title: What makes a merger worth doing?
detail: Mergers and Acquisitions · Case seminar
terms: Consider a distributor that a French manufacturer wants to acquire. The manufacturer can eliminate duplicated warehousing, while its chief executive would also be paid more for running a larger group. Both motives predict a bid. They predict different patterns after closing.

title: How can earnings rise when a buyer loses value?
detail: Mergers and Acquisitions · Case seminar
terms: A bidder trading at a high earnings multiple issues shares to buy a lower-multiple target. Reported earnings per share rise mechanically. The buyer still has to ask how much of the combined business it gave away.

title: Who gained on announcement day?
detail: Mergers and Acquisitions · Case seminar
terms: An event study asks how much a security moved relative to a model of its normal return. A target’s gain may reflect a transfer from the buyer. Use pre-announcement market values to measure the two shareholder groups on a common basis.

title: An overseas bid with a fixed euro budget
detail: Mergers and Acquisitions · Case seminar
terms: A French buyer agrees a headline price of IDR 1.8 trillion for an Indonesian target. Its euro financing commitment is €105m, and closing fees use €3m. Suppose all funds are needed on closing day. The currency in the signed offer determines the buyer’s funding exposure.

title: Why can a higher interest rate earn a bank less?
detail: Lending and Credit Analysis · Case seminar
terms: A bank cannot observe every borrower’s type. Changing its rate changes which applicants accept. This is the core intuition of equilibrium credit rationing and is distinct from the question of whether one already-approved borrower can afford a rate increase.

title: How large a loan can this exporter carry?
detail: Lending and Credit Analysis · Case seminar
terms: A lender is considering a new euro facility for an exporter. All amounts are annual and in millions of euros. The lending policy in this fictional case requires cash available for debt service to be at least 1.25 times scheduled interest and principal.

title: What loan rate pays for default risk?
detail: Lending and Credit Analysis · Case seminar
terms: One-year bullet loans have a simple model that exposes the difference between expected principal loss and a break-even promised rate. The payoff in default must be specified before the formula has meaning.

title: What changes when the borrower changes?
detail: Lending and Credit Analysis · Case seminar
terms: Underwriting a company, a household and a private-bank client all involves repayment and loss. The relevant evidence differs. Start by naming the expected source of repayment, then choose the measure that tests it.

title: Foreign exchange and trade
detail: France and Indonesia · International case
terms: A French importer owes a fixed number of rupiah. It buys those rupiah with euros, so a fall in rupiah per euro makes the invoice more expensive. A forward contract sets today the future rate for a specified date and amount.

title: Credit and trade
detail: India and the United Arab Emirates · International case
terms: A bank can lend against specific invoices if it can identify which qualify and collect from the customer. An Indian exporter selling to a UAE buyer may have domestic expenses in rupees and invoice proceeds in dollars. Invoice quality and currency exposure are separate sources of risk.

title: Capital-market research
detail: Indonesia and a regional comparator · International case
terms: An event study compares the return investors observed with a benchmark for what they might otherwise have earned. The choice of comparator can change the conclusion. Here both index returns have been converted to the same currency over the same trading interval.

title: Sovereign finance
detail: Chile and Brazil · International case
terms: A government’s debt ratio compares debt with annual national output. The primary deficit excludes interest payments. Foreign-currency debt adds a valuation channel when domestic currency weakens. The numbers here are for two hypothetical contracts in a regional comparison.

title: Infrastructure finance
detail: South Africa · International case
terms: Project lenders often look primarily to the project’s cash instead of relying on its owners. A South African power project earning rand but servicing a dollar loan has a currency mismatch: a weaker rand raises required debt payments even if output is unchanged.

title: Market microstructure
detail: Singapore and Japan · International case
terms: A displayed offer can apply to only a limited number of shares. Large orders walk through more than one price. The difference from a price observed when the investor made the decision is one component of implementation shortfall.

title: Asset management
detail: Australia and global markets · International case
terms: A scheme with benefits due in Australian dollars must translate gains on overseas shares into the currency it spends. Even a rising foreign equity market can lose money once translated. Use matched opening and closing exchange rates.

title: Valuation and deal evidence
detail: United States and Europe · International case
terms: A bidder can estimate future savings using a model; market prices tell a different piece of the story by measuring how investors revalued the two firms. Align currencies, dates and claims before comparing them.

title: Present value, merger surplus and the maximum bid
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: Paying a seller moves wealth between owners. It creates economic value only if the combination changes the future cash flows or the risk attached to them.

title: Why two interest rates imply a forward exchange rate
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: Two paths to the same certain future payment should cost the same when both can be traded on identical terms. Write down the units before manipulating the formula.

title: How loan losses enter the promised interest rate
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: The borrower promises a rate on the full loan. The bank collects that promised interest only in the states where it is paid.

title: Why diversification changes variance
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: Portfolio profits add across holdings. Their variances generally do not, because losses may arrive at the same time or offset one another.

title: How sovereign debt can rise despite a primary surplus
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: A debt ratio depends on both what a government owes and the size of the economy that supports it. Interest and growth act on different parts of the ratio.

title: How an announcement becomes an empirical estimate
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: An event-day return mixes news about the firm with market-wide movements. An event study defines a model of the normal return and measures the surprise relative to it.

title: From a random share price to the option-pricing equation
detail: Mathematical finance · Theory note
terms: If an option’s random movement can be offset by trading shares, the locally hedged position must earn the financing rate in the frictionless model. Stochastic calculus makes this statement precise.

title: Who gains when a merger is announced?
detail: M&A · Research discussion
terms: Read the finding, examine its limits, and design a way to test a stronger claim.

title: What does a lasting banking relationship provide?
detail: Lending · Research discussion
terms: Read the finding, examine its limits, and design a way to test a stronger claim.

title: Independent research project
detail: Research methods · Capstone
terms: Design an independent study around one answerable finance question. Document the data, analysis, alternative explanation and conclusion.

title: Merger bid and buyer value
detail: Interactive model
terms: Change the offer and the value of expected savings. See how every additional euro offered shifts the deal’s gains between the two sets of shareholders.

title: Loan repayment coverage
detail: Interactive model
terms: Change cash generation and debt payments to decide whether a borrower could pay on time and still meet the lender’s minimum coverage.

title: One-period option pricing
detail: Interactive model
terms: Build a small two-state market. Change the exercise price or interest rate and see which cash flows a call option pays in each state.

terms: An investment fund must decide how much ownership to buy.

terms: A finance director has to choose between opening a plant and expanding a distributor network.

terms: A group sells in rupiah, pays suppliers in dollars and reports in euros.

title: Investment and wealth management
detail: A mandate, allocation and performance attribution
terms: A client needs a stable income stream and can tolerate only limited losses.

title: Global markets, execution and risk
detail: An execution study and a risk-limit decision
terms: A trading desk needs to reduce risk before a bond issue settles.

title: Development and infrastructure finance
detail: Project sizing, risk allocation and development impact
terms: A lender is reviewing a solar plant funded in two currencies.

detail: A country comparison and reproducible debt stress test
terms: A sovereign analyst is asked whether a government can refinance next year.

title: Quantitative investment research
detail: A reproducible research paper and cost-aware backtest
terms: An asset manager wants to know whether a published signal survives trading costs.

title: Pricing and model validation
detail: Independent pricing, convergence tests and hedge validation
terms: A bank introduces a new option-pricing model.

title: Equity and debt capital markets
detail: A pricing recommendation, allocation rationale and reconciliation of issuer proceeds
terms: What price funds the company and leaves an executable order book?

title: Accretion and dilution
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: In merger analysis, a rise or fall in the buyer’s earnings per share after the transaction. Shareholder value is a separate calculation.

title: Adverse selection
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract can attract a different mix of applicants when people know more about their own quality or risk than the other side knows.

title: Agency problem
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: People acting on behalf of someone else can have different goals and better information about their own decisions.

title: Asset
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Something owned or controlled that can provide future value, such as cash, an invoice owed to you or equipment.

title: Asset pricing
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Studying how risk, time and market conditions relate to the prices and expected returns of investments.

title: Backtest
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A historical simulation of decisions made under an explicit rule, using information available at each date.

title: Balance of payments
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A country’s record of economic transactions between its residents and the rest of the world during a period.

title: Basis point
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: One hundredth of a percentage point. A rise from 4.00% to 4.01% is one basis point.

title: Benchmark
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A reference chosen in advance for comparison, such as a market index or an equal-weight portfolio.

title: Bid-offer spread
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The gap between the highest quoted buying price and the lowest quoted selling price.

title: Blended finance
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Combining public or philanthropic funding with commercial funding to support a development objective.

title: Bond
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A loan that can be bought and sold. Its terms say when the borrower must pay interest and repay the amount borrowed.

title: Bookbuilding
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Collecting indications of investor demand at proposed prices before deciding the terms and allocations of a securities offering.

title: Bookrunner
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The bank responsible for managing an offering’s order book and coordinating the pricing and allocation process.

title: Borrowing base
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A lending limit calculated from eligible collateral after applying agreed advance rates and deductions.

title: Calibration
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Choosing model parameters so that the model reproduces specified market observations as closely as possible.

title: Capital asset pricing model (CAPM)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A model that relates an asset’s expected return above the risk-free rate to its exposure to the wider market. That exposure is called beta.

title: Cash buffer
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Money kept available to meet upcoming bills or unexpected payments.

title: Cash flow
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Money actually entering or leaving an account over a period.

title: Collateral
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Cash or assets pledged to protect the other party if an obligation is missed.

title: Compound interest
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Interest earned on earlier interest as well as the starting amount.

title: Constant currency
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Recalculating results at a common set of exchange rates to examine operating changes across periods.

title: Convexity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Curvature. In fixed income it describes how a bond’s price sensitivity to yield changes as the yield moves.

title: Correlation
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A measure of how closely two series move together in a linear pattern.

title: Counterfactual
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: What would probably have happened without the event, decision or policy being studied.

title: Counterparty
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The other party to a financial contract or trade.

title: Coupon
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The interest payment specified in a bond’s terms.

title: Covenant
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A promise or condition in a financing agreement, such as maintaining an agreed level of cash.

title: Covered interest parity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A relationship connecting cash exchange rates, forward rates and interest rates in two currencies under matched, idealized funding terms.

title: Credit rationing
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A lender limits the amount available even when some applicants would accept the quoted terms or offer to pay more.

title: Credit spread
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Extra yield over a chosen reference yield. Credit risk, liquidity and market conditions can all affect it.

title: Currency quote
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The number of units of one named currency exchanged for one unit of another. The order determines whether to multiply or divide.

title: Debt service coverage ratio (DSCR)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Cash available to meet scheduled debt payments divided by the principal and interest due for the period.

title: Derivative
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract whose value depends on something else, such as a currency, an interest rate or a share price.

title: Discount factor
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The price today of one unit of currency payable at a particular future date under specified risk assumptions.

title: Discount rate
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Rate used to express a future payment in today’s money, reflecting time and the relevant risk.

title: Discounted cash flow (DCF)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A valuation method that brings a series of future cash flows back to a common date.

title: Diversification
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Combining exposures that do not always move together to reduce dependence on a single outcome.

title: Dividend
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A payment a company makes to shareholders from available resources.

title: Duration
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A measure used to estimate how strongly a bond price responds to a small interest-rate change.

title: DV01
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Change in value associated with a one-basis-point shift in a specified rate or curve. Document the sign convention.

title: EBITDA
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Check how the seller calculates and adjusts this measure.

title: Eigenvector
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A direction that a linear transformation stretches or shrinks without changing its direction. In finance it can describe common movements in several assets.

title: Enterprise value
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Value of the business operations attributable to its capital providers. A bridge adjusts it to the amount due to shareholders.

title: Enterprise-to-equity bridge
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A schedule showing how the value of business operations becomes the amount attributable to common shareholders.

title: Equity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The owners’ claim after liabilities are deducted from assets. It also means ownership shares.

title: Exchange-rate regime
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: How authorities manage their currency, ranging from a fixed link to a market-driven rate.

title: Expected credit loss
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: For a simple single-period example, default probability multiplied by exposure and the share lost if default occurs.

title: Expected shortfall
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The average loss in a specified worst fraction of outcomes.

title: Expected utility
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The probability-weighted average satisfaction from possible outcomes. It permits comparing choices when money has different value in different states.

title: Exposure at default (EAD)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Amount at risk when a borrower defaults. It can include draws on a previously unused facility.

title: Financial due diligence
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Checking a business’s earnings, cash needs and debt before a transaction.

title: Foreign exchange (FX)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The conversion of one currency into another. Always state how the rate is quoted.

title: Forward
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract to exchange an agreed amount at a set price on a future date.

title: FP&A
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Financial planning and analysis. The team builds budgets and forecasts and explains business performance.

title: Free float
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The shares considered available for public trading under the venue or index provider’s definition.

title: Goodwill
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: In a simple purchase of an entire company, the part of the purchase price above the measured value of identifiable net assets.

title: Greeks
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Measures of how an option’s value changes with an input. Delta measures its sensitivity to the underlying price.

title: Greenshoe
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: An overallotment option that allows underwriters to buy additional shares on agreed terms to cover an overallocation.

title: Hedge
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A position or contract intended to reduce an identified exposure, such as the cost of paying in a foreign currency.

title: IFRS and US GAAP
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Two sets of financial reporting rules. IFRS stands for International Financial Reporting Standards. US GAAP means US Generally Accepted Accounting Principles.

title: Initial public offering (IPO)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A company’s first public offering of shares. The shares may be newly issued, sold by existing holders, or both.

title: Interest rate
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The price of borrowing money or the return for lending it, quoted as a percentage over a stated period.

title: IPO underpricing
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: In empirical IPO studies, a positive return from the offer price to the first trading close. The meaning depends on the price benchmark.

title: Leveraged buyout (LBO)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A purchase funded partly with debt, usually with the acquired business’s cash helping repay it.

title: Liability
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Something owed to another party, such as a loan or an unpaid supplier bill.

title: Liquidity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Access to cash when payments fall due. For a security, it also describes how easily it can be traded at a reasonable price.

title: Look-ahead bias
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Accidental use of information in a test before a decision-maker could have known it.

title: Loss given default (LGD)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The fraction of exposure lost if a borrower defaults, after the recoveries included in the chosen definition.

title: Margin
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: In business accounts, profit expressed relative to sales. In derivatives trading, margin is collateral required to support a position.

title: Market microstructure
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: How orders, trading venues and dealer behaviour affect the prices and costs of a trade.

title: Martingale
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A process whose expected future value, given current information, equals its current value under the specified probability measure.

title: Monte Carlo simulation
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Estimating an outcome by generating many possible paths and summarizing the results.

title: Moral hazard
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract can change behaviour after it is signed when the other party cannot fully observe or control those actions.

title: Net present value (NPV)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Today’s value of incoming cash minus today’s value of outgoing cash.

title: New issue concession
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The extra yield a new bond offers compared with the estimated fair yield on comparable outstanding debt.

title: No-arbitrage
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A pricing condition that rules out a feasible trade producing a certain gain for no net investment and with no risk of loss.

title: Option
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract giving the buyer a right to buy or sell on stated terms. The buyer pays a premium for the right.

title: Overfitting
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Learning patterns peculiar to one sample that fail to hold up on new data.

title: Payable
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Money a business owes a supplier for goods or services already received.

title: Percentage point
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The difference between two percentages. A rate rising from 4% to 5% rises one percentage point.

title: Perpetuity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A stream of payments assumed to continue indefinitely under the model.

title: Present value (PV)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: An amount at a future date expressed in today’s money using a rate suited to its timing and risk.

title: Primary balance
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Government revenue minus non-interest spending under the sign convention used in this course.

title: Primary repayment source
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The cash a lender expects will repay a loan in the normal course, such as operating receipts or household income.

title: Primary shares
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: New shares issued by the company. Their sale brings money into the company and increases the outstanding share count.

title: Principal
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The amount borrowed or invested before interest is added.

title: Probability of default (PD)
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The chance that the borrower meets the specified default definition over the stated horizon.

title: Profit
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Revenue left after the expenses recognized for the period.

title: Purchasing power parity
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A comparison of what a common basket costs in different currencies. It offers a reference point for comparing price levels.

title: Receivable
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Money a customer owes for a sale already made.

title: Regression
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A way of estimating how an outcome varies with one or more observed inputs.

title: Replicating portfolio
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A combination of traded claims that delivers the same future cash flows as a contract in every state covered by the model.

title: Revenue
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Amount earned by selling goods or services. The customer may pay later.

title: Rights issue
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: An offer allowing current shareholders to subscribe for new shares in proportion to an existing holding, under the stated terms.

title: Risk factor
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A common source of variation in returns, such as market movements or a change in interest rates.

title: Risk premium
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Extra expected return for bearing risk, or the amount a risk-averse person would give up to replace a gamble with certainty, depending on context.

title: Risk-neutral valuation
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A way of pricing by taking a discounted expectation under a probability model consistent with traded prices.

title: Rule of priority
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The assumed order in which claims receive available proceeds. In a real case, contract terms and local law matter.

title: Secondary shares
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Existing shares sold by their holder. The sale transfers ownership and the seller receives the proceeds.

title: Sensitivity analysis
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Varying an assumption to see how the answer or decision changes.

title: Settlement
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: The final transfer of cash or securities needed to complete a transaction.

title: Share
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A unit of ownership in a company. A shareholder may receive dividends and may gain or lose money if its price changes.

title: Standard error
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: An estimate of how much a statistic would vary across repeated samples under the assumed sampling process.

title: Stochastic calculus
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Mathematics for working with quantities that change continuously and randomly.

title: Sukuk
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Islamic finance certificates linked to an underlying asset, use or investment. The contract determines holders’ rights and payments.

title: Swap
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: A contract to exchange payment streams, such as fixed interest for floating interest.

title: Synergy
detail: Plain-English definition
terms: Extra value expected from combining businesses, such as a saving attainable only after a merger.

title: Theoretical ex-rights price (TERP)
detail: Plain-English definition

title: Transactions and double entry
detail: F01 · Lesson 1 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Each event changes at least two accounts. Borrowing increases cash and debt together, so it creates no immediate profit. Whose books are open? A founder pays €600 personally for a machine used by a newly formed business. One payment creates different records for the founder and for the business. The business controls a machine and either owes its founder €600 or has received an owner contribution. The agreement determines which. The founder’s private bank account never enters the business ledger. The accounting entity is the boundary around the transactions being measured. Ask who controls the resource, who owes the obligation, and whether cash moved inside that boundary. An invoice, bank statement and contribution agreement answer different parts of those questions. A cash receipt on its own seldom tells you whether its source is a sale, loan or investment. How debits reach the statements Debit and credit mean left and right in a two-sided account. Assets generally increase on the debit side. Liabilities and contributed capital generally increase on the credit side. Revenue increases owners’ residual earnings and normally has a credit balance. Expenses reduce those earnings and normally have a debit balance. A journal is the dated record of both sides. Posting carries those sides to the individual ledger accounts. At period-end a trial balance lists their totals. Equal debits and credits tell you the arithmetic fits. They cannot detect an entire missing transaction, a duplicated balanced entry or an amount posted to the wrong expense. Sales can require two entries Consider a shop that hands over completed goods and gives the customer thirty days to pay. One entry records the customer’s promise and the revenue. A second removes goods from inventory and records their cost. The resulting profit belongs to the period of sale even if no cash comes in that day. Collection later increases cash and reduces the receivable. On the other hand an unpaid supplier balance is a liability. Paying that supplier uses cash and reduces what the shop owes. Re-reading each event from the shop’s viewpoint keeps customers’ promises and the shop’s own promises on different sides. Build a small ledger A weekend bicycle stall

title: The balance sheet
detail: F01 · Lesson 2 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Assets show resources controlled at a date. Liabilities are obligations. Equity is the residual owners would claim at the reported carrying values. A dated statement and a period of change Imagine signing a contract on 31 December and receiving the bank proceeds on 2 January. A balance sheet is tied to the stated date. The underlying rights and obligations as they exist on that date govern recognition. A list of what happened during January cannot simply be added to the December balances. A statement of changes or a cash flow statement explains movements between two snapshots. An asset ending €5,000 higher might reflect purchases of €20,000 and sales of €15,000. The net change alone cannot reveal either gross flow. Ask for opening balances and transaction detail when the question concerns activity. What capital can absorb Equity is the difference between recorded assets and liabilities. An unexpected asset write-down reduces this cushion before all creditors necessarily suffer a loss. A firm with positive equity can nevertheless fail to pay on time if most of its assets consist of long-lived equipment that cannot be sold promptly for their book amount. Liquidity concerns access to funds when payments come due. Solvency concerns the capacity of the asset base and future business to support obligations overall. Compare genuinely available liquid resources with a maturity schedule. Cash pledged to guarantee another contract may not be available to pay tomorrow’s supplier. Working capital as a first screen A common indicator is current assets minus current liabilities. Items expected to turn into cash or be settled in the near term enter their respective groups under the applicable classification rules. This subtraction can reveal a financing gap, but two firms with the same number can face quite different timing. Read individual lines. A fresh customer invoice due before payday has a different liquidity profile from old inventory with no buyer. Longer supplier terms can help fund inventory today but create a concentration of bills next month. A business receiving cash up front can operate for long periods with negative working capital. Read a maturity mismatch A clinic with valuable equipment

title: Revenue and expenses
detail: F01 · Lesson 3 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Recognize a sale when the relevant performance occurs. Match the cost of the goods sold to the sale and separate that event from payment. Find the promised goods or service A club sells a twelve-month membership for one payment. The member is buying access throughout the year. A shop selling a sealed camera usually promises something different, a good whose control passes at a particular point. Dates of order, invoicing, delivery and cash transfer can therefore give four different answers to when revenue arises. Identify the customer, what has been promised, the amount earned and evidence of fulfilment. For simple services delivered evenly, elapsed time can measure performance. A large deposit alone gives no evidence of service already provided. If the service pattern is uneven, counting months mechanically may misstate how much work has been supplied. Separate the bill from the work Cash before performance creates a customer advance, often called deferred revenue or a contract liability. Performance before unconditional collection can give rise to an asset. In a simple completed credit sale where only the passage of time remains before payment, the asset is a receivable. Different contract conditions require further analysis. In the next period the liability decreases as the seller delivers. Collection of an existing receivable simply changes which asset the seller holds. Compare movements in advances and receivables with reported revenue to understand whether growth reflects delivery, advance sales, or a buildup of customer credit. What becomes an expense The cost of an item sold leaves inventory when that sale is recognized. Costs of services consumed in the period can become expenses even before a supplier invoices the business. If a payment buys a right to future service, an unused portion can remain a prepaid asset. A useful test asks what resource remains at period-end and whether the business still controls it. A paid insurance policy with six unused months has a future benefit. An advert that has already run generally does not give the firm an identifiable remaining service, even if managers hope it raises future sales. Construct a timing bridge A prepaid maintenance agreement

title: Cash flow and reconciliation
detail: F01 · Lesson 4 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Start with profit, reverse noncash items and adjust for amounts unpaid or uncollected. Explain how a profitable firm can use cash. Two routes to operating cash A business can calculate cash from operations by summing customer receipts and cash paid to suppliers and staff. This direct route asks what actually passed through the bank for ordinary trading. The indirect route starts from accrual profit and removes timing and noncash effects to reach the same operating amount. If the routes disagree, inspect the period covered, classification of cash flows and whether gross or net balances were used. Gains on asset sales may appear in profit although the sale proceeds belong in investing cash flows. Remove the gain on the indirect bridge, then show actual proceeds once in investing. Turn balance movements back into cash If every sale is on credit, a simplified receivable account starts with the opening amount, adds sales, subtracts collections and closes at the ending balance. Rearranging yields collections = sales + opening receivables − closing receivables. Write-offs, foreign currency translation and acquired receivables can also change the balance in real accounts. Inventory introduces a second bridge. Purchases = cost of goods sold + closing inventory − opening inventory, under simple cost assumptions. Supplier cash paid equals purchases + opening trade payables − closing trade payables if everything is bought on credit. Work each account separately before combining the signs. Read weak cash conversion carefully One year of low operating cash can reflect valuable growth if new orders require inventory and short-term credit for customers. It can also reflect customers taking longer to pay or a business accumulating unsold goods. The same arithmetic supports different explanations, so compare it with sales growth, ageing schedules and subsequent collections. Cash from operations also moves when payment dates shift across a reporting boundary. Delaying suppliers can improve current cash while making next month harder. When comparing years, normalize the trading calendar and see whether the underlying cash cycle is improving or the firm merely borrowed time from suppliers. title: Inventory and fixed assets
detail: F01 · Lesson 5 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Buying stock delays an expense until sale. Buying equipment usually spreads its cost over its useful life through depreciation. Which units left the shelf? A grocer buys identical bottles at several prices. Selling one bottle requires assigning a cost to the sale and a cost to what remains. A first-in, first-out cost formula, commonly called FIFO, assigns the earliest purchases to cost of goods sold. A weighted-average formula shares the cost across units available under the chosen averaging period. Both allocations can describe the same sales proceeds and physical quantities. When purchase prices rise over time, FIFO generally assigns older, lower unit costs to the sale and larger amounts to ending inventory than an average formula. That difference affects both gross margin and the value shown on the balance sheet. Cost recovery and selling value Inventory that is damaged or obsolete may no longer recover its recorded cost. In a lower-of-cost-and-net-realizable-value example, estimate the selling price less the costs still needed to finish and sell the item. Compare that amount with its recorded cost to determine whether a write-down is needed. Equipment creates a different pattern. Its capitalized cost includes amounts necessary to prepare it for its intended use in this example. Spread depreciable cost, or cost less estimated residual value, over useful life once available for use. Routine maintenance consumed in ordinary running generally creates a current expense. Changing an estimate A truck may wear out faster than expected. Starting from its carrying amount at the date of reassessment, allocate the revised remaining depreciable amount over the revised remaining useful life. A revised estimate changes the pattern going forward in this example. It does not require erasing the original depreciation merely because new evidence arrived. Examine use records, maintenance plans, expected resale proceeds and management’s prior estimates. A firm can increase current earnings by extending lives in a model. An analyst should compare the new assumption with physical use and peers before accepting the interpretation as improved operating performance. title: Receivables and estimates
detail: F01 · Lesson 6 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: A customer invoice is an asset only to the extent it is collectible. Compare a closing allowance with ageing and subsequent cash receipts. Estimate losses before cash runs out A supplier credits customers for thirty days. Some will pay the full invoice, some part, and some none. The gross receivable records the contractual amounts. The loss allowance is a separate balance that reduces the carrying amount to reflect expected shortfalls under the measurement approach used. Grouping customers by overdue status can be a useful starting model. Customers sharing an age band may still differ in collateral, location or financial condition. Historical collection rates need adjustment when current evidence says tomorrow’s losses may differ. Document assumptions separately from factual balances so a reviewer can see where judgment started. Separate an expense from an allowance An allowance is the stock of estimated losses at a date. The impairment expense is a flow during the period. If an amount already allowed for is finally written off, reduce the gross receivable and the allowance together. This consumes the earlier estimate without automatically creating another expense at write-off. With no recoveries or other movements, closing allowance = opening allowance + impairment expense − write-offs. The expense needed to reach a target therefore equals closing target − opening allowance + write-offs. This reconciliation is especially important when a year has large write-offs. Comparing closing allowance with opening allowance alone understates new loss recognition. Test the estimate against evidence Payments received after the balance-sheet date can help assess whether a year-end estimate was reasonable, depending on what they reveal about conditions at that date. Separate a genuinely new event from confirmation of an existing problem. Ask what an analyst could reasonably have known at the time. Also examine concentration. A large balance due from one struggling buyer can deserve a separate estimate before applying percentage rates to the remaining pool. Counting that customer both individually and in a pool duplicates exposure. Aggressive assumptions about a major client can obscure a deterioration even when average overdue days appear stable. title: Debt, leases and equity
detail: F01 · Lesson 7 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Separate finance charges from repayment of principal. Compare financing obligations using both the balance sheet and the accompanying notes. Read the funding promise A shareholder can receive dividends if the business distributes money. A lender normally has contractual rights to interest and principal. Some instruments mix features, so begin with the actual payment terms rather than their marketing names. A long maturity does not remove an obligation to pay, while an ordinary share need not require future redemption. Separate three exam questions. What amount is recorded at the reporting date? How much finance cost arose during the period? What cash must be found by each future date? A single total cannot answer all three. Principal instalments, maturity dates and fixed or floating terms determine whether accounting expense corresponds closely to the near-term payment. Why present value appears in a lease A lessee may gain the right to use equipment for several periods while committing to future rentals. In a simple recognized lease, the initial liability is the present value of unpaid contractual payments, discounted using the rate specified for the exercise. With no other adjustments, the right-of-use asset can start at the same amount. Each period, interest builds on the opening liability and the cash payment reduces it. The right-of-use asset is depreciated under its own schedule. Thus the amount reducing the liability is different from the expense charged for using the equipment. Actual recognition rules depend on the applicable standard and the facts. Compare a loan with a rental commitment A business using leased vans can appear different from one using identical vans bought with borrowed money. Include recognized lease liabilities consistently when constructing financing measures. Check maturity schedules for both forms of funding and identify contract payments omitted from a simplified estimate. Equity can be substantial yet offer few funds with which to pay the next instalment. A creditor evaluating rollover risk, the risk of being unable to refinance maturing debt, examines committed cash and borrowing lines along with likely future funding costs. A company with a large bullet repayment has concentrated that risk in one date. Unpack a financing schedule Two rentals on a small press

title: Groups and currencies
detail: F01 · Lesson 8 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Trace a parent’s ownership of a subsidiary, eliminate internal sales and distinguish the currency of operations from the currency used to present group accounts. Which company belongs in the group? A consolidated group treats a controlling parent and its controlled subsidiaries as one reporting unit. Control in the simple examples means the parent can direct relevant activities and is exposed to economic returns. A shareholding percentage is evidence but contracts and voting arrangements can change the assessment. With partial ownership, an entity can still control a subsidiary and consolidate its assets and liabilities in full. The share of net assets or earnings attributable to outside owners is then identified as a non-controlling interest. Confusing ownership share with consolidation perimeter can lead an analyst to remove real group assets or include outside companies. Strip out trading inside the perimeter When a parent sells inventory to a subsidiary, one member records revenue and another records a purchase. Viewed from the group’s perspective the goods have only changed location. Clear the internal trade and any matching receivable and payable. Earnings on unsold goods still inside the group are unrealized externally. If only some units have been sold to outsiders, identify which proportion of the internal margin remains in closing inventory. Remove that portion from both inventory carrying value and group profit. The profit on units sold externally is ultimately measured from the original external purchase cost to the outside selling price. Currencies can change the story Operational currency and reporting currency need not coincide. A subsidiary may invoice, pay staff and borrow in one main functional currency, while the group presents in another. Translation converts numbers for presentation. A separate issue arises when a company itself owes a fixed amount in a currency different from its functional currency. For an introductory analytical comparison, convert foreign sales using the exchange-rate basis specified in the exercise. To study growth at constant currency, value both periods at one common rate. Actual consolidated reporting uses account-specific translation conventions. A movement in translated sales alone cannot show whether more products were sold. title: Financial ratios
detail: F01 · Lesson 9 · Financial Accounting and Statement Analysis
terms: Decompose return on equity into profit margin, asset turnover and financial leverage. Improving return on equity can reflect higher debt as well as better trading. What question does a ratio answer? A buyer comparing retailers asks whether one earns more from each sale, generates more sales from its assets, or uses more borrowing. Each question uses a different denominator. Net margin divides net income by sales, turnover divides sales by average assets, and financial leverage divides average assets by average equity. Use an average balance when comparing a full-period flow with a stock that can change during the year. The simple mean of opening and closing balances is an approximation. If assets were acquired on the final day, that mean can overstate the capital actually in use throughout the year. Keep the numerator and denominator aligned Return on equity is best interpreted for the same claimants on both sides. In a simple single-owner business, net income divided by average equity fits. In a group with outside minority owners, mixing parent-attributable income and the whole group’s equity produces a ratio that does not correspond clearly to either group of investors. The DuPont decomposition is an identity, an arithmetic relationship when the same definitions are used throughout. It is not a causal model. More leverage can increase return when operating returns exceed funding costs, but new interest expense or falling margins can reverse that result. Tiny or negative equity makes the ratio especially hard to interpret. Evaluate growth in context Ratios compare proportions and can hide changes in scale. A firm can grow euro profit while its margin falls if it sells sufficiently more. Sales can also rise temporarily when unusually generous credit terms pull future business into the current period. Ask how quickly customers pay and whether inventory rises alongside the growth. Cross-check a ratio with an adjacent measure. A rising return on equity accompanied by flat margins, weakening cash conversion and a shrinking equity base suggests a different explanation from one driven by stronger products. A useful answer distinguishes what the ratios prove arithmetically from what requires evidence in the financial statements. Decompose and interpret Two firms earning the same profit

title: Opportunity cost
detail: F02 · Lesson 1 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Using capital for a warehouse means giving up the next-best use of that money. The economic cost includes that forgone benefit. The choice determines the cost Suppose a furniture maker already owns a workshop. Using it on a new contract requires no cheque for rent, but occupying it prevents a tenant from paying for it. Economic cost measures resources given up by choosing one action rather than the best feasible alternative. Accounting records alone do not always reveal that sacrifice. List mutually exclusive choices and say whose decision is being evaluated. Using a worker’s evening to make a product might displace paid overtime, family time or nothing the worker values equally. The relevant cost is the best available alternative for that evening, not the sum of every imaginable alternative. Sunk costs, recoverable costs and space A paid design fee with no resale value is sunk when deciding whether to produce the designed item. One can still decide whether to incur future production costs. By contrast, material bought years ago can have a current opportunity cost if it could be sold or would otherwise have to be replaced. Ask what would actually happen to each resource if the project were declined. If specialized stock would be discarded for a disposal fee, using it can even avoid a cost. If the same stock is needed for a confirmed alternative order, using it here could force a replacement purchase. Its historical invoice answers neither question by itself. When a constraint binds A machine running at capacity puts a value on each additional hour. An order using that time may displace the contribution from another order. Contribution is revenue less costs that change when the activity occurs. Idle capacity has a different opportunity cost, provided accepting the order creates no other credible sacrifice. A calculation can be correct for today but wrong for a longer decision. A salaried worker may be available for one short special order with no new cash cost. Repeated commitments can require hiring or displace regular work. State the decision horizon and show the assumption making the resource available at that horizon. Price the next-best alternative An unused production die

title: Marginal choice
detail: F02 · Lesson 2 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Compare the extra benefit and cost of the next unit. A profitable business can still lose money by expanding one unit too far. Incremental revenue and cost A restaurant is considering opening for one more evening each week. The question is how the restaurant’s total receipts and costs change with that evening. Include wages for a new shift, extra power and food. Allocated shares of unchanged monthly rent will affect the restaurant’s accounts but do not change the immediate choice. Marginal analysis compares two nearby plans. When units are indivisible, compare total outcomes with and without the next unit. For a smooth quantity choice, the familiar condition marginal benefit equals marginal cost describes an interior optimum under suitable curvature. At a capacity limit, or where costs jump, the best feasible quantity can occur at a boundary. A fixed cost can become avoidable A cost is fixed relative to a specified range and time horizon. Suppose a kitchen can serve 50 customers with one cook but needs an entire second shift for customer 51. The apparent cost of an isolated sandwich understates the cost of crossing that staffing threshold. Calculate the whole block of extra orders if they come together. The reverse situation also occurs. Closing for one day might save ingredients yet leave all contracted staffing costs payable. A decision to close an entire location for a year can release those commitments. Use the resource change associated with the choice in front of you and explain which commitments persist. Capacity and displaced business If an additional low-price booking uses the last available slot, include the contribution sacrificed on a displaced full-price booking. Use contribution after the costs avoided by losing it. If displacement is uncertain, estimate the expected value of the alternative on the available information at the decision date. A positive marginal contribution can justify a temporary order without implying that its price supports the business over the long run. The business eventually needs revenue to replace equipment and finance new commitments. State explicitly whether you are solving a one-off utilization decision or a continuing pricing decision. Compare complete plans A print shop’s night shift

title: Demand and elasticity
detail: F02 · Lesson 3 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Elasticity measures how sensitive quantity is to price. It helps explain why a price increase can raise or lower sales revenue. Movement along a demand curve If a cinema changes its own price while alternatives, incomes, preferences and showtimes stay fixed, the quantity response is a movement along its demand curve. If a new festival attracts people to the area during the same week, that event can shift the demand curve itself. Observed price and quantity changes mix both mechanisms. A price elasticity divides a percentage change in quantity by a percentage change in price. It is unit-free, so ticket offices using euros or cents obtain the same answer. A slope expressed as seats per euro is different. On a straight demand line the slope can stay constant even as elasticity changes with the level of price and sales. How to interpret the magnitude With ordinary downward-sloping demand the elasticity is negative, and people often discuss its absolute magnitude. A magnitude above one describes a proportionately large response. Near a given point a small price rise then lowers total revenue. When the magnitude is below one, a small increase can raise revenue. The midpoint formula provides a consistent finite-interval calculation. Revenue and profit need separate checks. More ticket sales may require expensive venue changes or incur royalties per seat. At the price that maximizes revenue, a further sale may still cost enough to reduce profit. When actual price-quantity pairs are known, compute total revenue and variable costs directly for both endpoints. Substitutes, time and evidence A commuter can switch travel time sooner than she can move house. Long-run demand responses can therefore differ from short-run responses. Market definition also matters. Switching from one cinema chain to another is easier than finding a substitute for all indoor entertainment. Elasticity estimated for one chain need not apply to the entire industry. A better estimate isolates price changes from other demand shocks. Compare similar locations over the same period or use a credible pricing experiment when available. If discounts are offered only during slow weeks, the observed discount and low attendance can wrongly suggest that a lower price reduced demand. Measure a finite price change Museum admissions

title: Market structure
detail: F02 · Lesson 4 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Contrast competitive price taking with market power. A firm with market power considers how selling another unit affects the price on its other units. The price-setting problem A price-taking producer assumes its own sales have negligible impact on market price. If producing an extra unit raises cost by €7 and market price is €9, that unit increases operating contribution by €2. Limited capacity and shutting down can still matter, but there is no price cut on units already sold. A firm setting one price for all customers faces an additional trade-off. To sell more units it may need to lower the price on every unit. Revenue gained from the additional customer is offset by revenue lost on earlier customers. Compare the change in total revenue with the change in total cost, rather than comparing the last quoted price with unit cost. Deriving marginal revenue Suppose inverse demand gives price P = a − bQ, where Q is quantity and a and b are positive constants. Total revenue is price times quantity, aQ − bQ². Differentiating with respect to Q yields marginal revenue a − 2bQ. It falls twice as fast as price in this linear example. With constant marginal cost c, an unconstrained interior choice sets a − 2bQ = c. Compute Q and then return to demand to find the price customers will pay. For indivisible products evaluate neighboring feasible quantities directly. If a capacity limit is below that interior output, compare feasible choices at the boundary. Market power and its limits Facing downward-sloping demand does not guarantee positive economic profit. Research costs, fixed production costs and the possibility of entry can absorb the margin. Close substitutes make buyers more willing to leave. A high market share suggests an investigation but does not itself measure how strongly a price increase would reduce sales. Price discrimination requires some ability to identify different willingness to pay and limit resale. A separate charge for an extra unit can allow extra sales without reducing the price to existing customers. That difference is why the single-price marginal-revenue formula should not be applied mechanically to a negotiated contract priced separately. Find a single-price optimum Specialized training seats

title: Choice through time
detail: F02 · Lesson 5 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: A budget links spending today with spending later. The interest rate determines the exchange between the two dates when borrowing and lending are available. Build the lifetime budget A student can move money between this term and next term. Saving reduces today’s consumption but increases next term’s spending power. Borrowing does the reverse. With one common rate r, the present value of consumption cannot exceed the present value of resources, assuming repayment is required and there are no gifts or other funds. Let y₀ and y₁ be resources available now and later and c₀ and c₁ consumption on those dates. If everything is eventually spent, c₁ = y₁ + (y₀ − c₀)(1+r). Its slope is −(1+r). Each extra euro consumed today gives up 1+r euros of future consumption, whether it reduces savings or increases borrowing under the common-rate assumption. Preferences through time The budget says which plans are affordable. It cannot tell you which one the student prefers. Time preference measures how much someone values consumption at one date against another. Expected income, urgent needs and the desire to smooth living standards can influence the choice. Two people with the same resources can therefore choose different plans. A rise in interest rates increases the reward to postponing consumption, a substitution effect. It also changes purchasing power relative to an existing plan. A net saver may feel richer, while a net borrower faces a higher cost. A prediction about total current consumption requires both effects and information on preferences. When borrowing and saving differ Real borrowers can face a loan rate higher than the rate earned on deposits. The budget line then has a corner at the endowment point where neither borrowing nor lending occurs. Points using savings follow the deposit rate and points needing borrowing follow the loan rate. A cap on debt can rule out some plans entirely. In an exam, begin with the direction of the transfer. A plan requiring money before income arrives may be valuable when discounted yet infeasible because no credit is available. Distinguish the value of a project with access to capital markets from this individual’s ability to finance it by the required date. Compare two-date plans Two rates for a family budget

title: Risk and expected utility
detail: F02 · Lesson 6 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Risk-averse people value an extra euro more when resources are scarce. They may prefer a certain payment to a gamble with the same average payout. Expected payoff and preferences A shop owner choosing insurance wants to know what resources remain after a loss. Compare possible final wealth, including initial savings, premium and losses in each state. Probability-weighted average wealth describes the average of many comparable outcomes. It is not necessarily the amount this individual would accept for surrendering a risky prospect. Expected utility assigns a number to each possible wealth level using the person’s preferences and then averages these utility numbers, weighted by probabilities. With a concave utility function, a euro gained when poor helps more than an extra euro gained when rich. Risk aversion in this model concerns the curvature of utility in final wealth. Certainty equivalents and willingness to insure Find the guaranteed wealth giving the same utility as the risky prospect. This is its certainty equivalent. The difference between expected wealth and the certainty equivalent is the risk premium. Risk-neutral people with linear utility have a zero risk premium in this framework, while strictly risk-averse people place a positive premium on eliminating genuine risk. For full insurance, the premium paid by the owner reduces wealth in both states and the policy replaces the entire covered loss. Set guaranteed insured wealth equal to the uninsured certainty equivalent to find the maximum acceptable insurance price. This can exceed the expected loss, which helps explain a market for insurance covering administration costs. What changes the comparison? Wealth matters. The same absolute loss can be much more damaging to a small business than a large diversified owner. Insurance might also exclude part of the loss or require a deductible, an initial portion paid by the owner. Then final wealth is still uncertain and each insured state must be valued separately. An expected-utility calculation depends on credible probabilities and the stated preference function. A result using square-root utility illustrates a decision rule for that person. It does not establish what every borrower or investor should choose. Explain whether more information would change probabilities, the payoffs themselves, or the preference assumptions. title: Adverse selection
detail: F02 · Lesson 7 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Before contracting, sellers or borrowers may know more about their quality. A price change can alter which applicants accept an offer. Pooling people with private information An insurer may see an applicant’s postcode but know less than the applicant about where the car will really be parked. Before a contract is agreed, people with different risk information can have different willingness to accept the offered terms. A pooled quote treats participating types alike even if their expected losses differ. An average using the population is valid only if participation leaves that population mix intact. When premiums rise, lower-risk customers may be first to leave. The average cost among those still buying rises, potentially requiring another price increase. A market need not unravel completely. Underwriting information, compulsory participation or sufficiently large willingness to pay can support pooling. Borrower participation and loan pricing A bank receives the promised repayment only in states where the borrower pays, plus any recovery on default. The borrower’s payoff distribution can make high-rate loans attractive to riskier types who expect either a large success or a loss largely borne by the lender. Recalculate expected receipts at each quote using the people actually accepting it. A lender can sometimes prefer rationing, turning down some applicants at an unchanged price, to raising the rate. Establishing this conclusion requires more than showing that rates are high. Show how acceptance changes, why expected net returns fall, and why demand remains above the amount of funding the lender is willing or able to supply. Screening, signaling and evidence Screening is action by the less-informed party to learn or separate types. A bank might offer a menu of interest and collateral terms to borrowers. Signaling is action by the informed party, such as investing in verifiable disclosure. A useful signal is easier or less costly for the type it is meant to identify. Collateral requirements can also exclude capable applicants who lack wealth. A drop in observed default rates after stricter screening could reflect changing composition instead of improved behaviour. To assess selection, examine applications, acceptances, rejections and type indicators before the money is released, including those who declined the quote. title: Moral hazard and agency
detail: F02 · Lesson 8 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: After receiving funds, a borrower may change behaviour. Monitoring, incentives and contract terms can alter the payoff from taking hidden risks. Different incentives after the agreement A lender approves a project on the understanding it will invest in reliable machinery. Once funds are released, the owner may undertake a more volatile venture. If the choice is hidden or difficult to enforce, the original terms can influence which action the owner takes. This is moral hazard after contracting. Agency problems arise when one person acts on behalf of someone with different interests. The fact that an outcome is bad does not establish misconduct or hidden action. A genuinely prudent project can fail. Identify the decision the agent could change, what the principal can observe, and how the contract changes the payoff from that decision. Divide project payoffs by the contract With simple debt of face value D and no other claims, a lender receives the smaller of project proceeds and D when it can claim all proceeds up to repayment. The owner receives the excess above D, floored at zero by limited liability. Project value is the sum of these two amounts in every state. Debt can make additional upside attractive to the owner while shifting part of the downside to the creditor. Calculate expected total proceeds for each action and separately calculate the private payoffs. A privately preferred action with a lower total expected value demonstrates the incentive conflict. Which party bears a loss depends on security, guarantees and bankruptcy costs. Changing incentives without eliminating the business A covenant constrains an activity, such as taking additional senior debt or investing outside an agreed line. Monitoring can detect breaches, while collateral or owner co-investment can change who pays when a project fails. Each arrangement can also create costs or prevent a good future decision under unforeseen conditions. Judge an intervention by comparing what it costs to implement with the loss it prevents. When behaviour is unobservable, monitoring must yield informative evidence in time to act. Guarantees need a guarantor able to pay in the bad state. A contractual promise that is impossible to enforce may make little difference to expected payoffs. Test debt-induced risk shifting A borrower with a shipping license

title: Bargaining and games
detail: F02 · Lesson 9 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: Compare each party’s alternatives if negotiations fail. A good project can collapse when parties cannot credibly commit to what they promise. Money on and off the bargaining table A baker and a delivery firm earn more by working together than apart. Their outside options are attainable payoffs if negotiations break down. A deal must generally offer each party at least its outside option to secure voluntary agreement. The remaining surplus can be divided in many ways. A negotiated price is only a transfer between the parties when it does not change total value, tax or incentives. Write total surplus first, then the distribution. If either side has a stronger alternative, the available bargaining surplus shrinks and the feasible set of agreements changes. A claim about fairness is separate from a calculation of willingness to accept. Solve sequential choices backward Some bargains span several decisions. A supplier may have to build a specialized tool today before bargaining over its use tomorrow. Backward induction means finding what the parties will choose at the final stage, then using those payoffs to evaluate the earlier decision. A promised threat matters only if carrying it out would be sensible when the time arrives. A relationship-specific investment can be worthwhile jointly yet unappealing to the party that must pay for it. After the investment is sunk, a partner can negotiate for a share of the created value. Anticipating this hold-up, the investor may refuse to invest. A credible minimum purchase or compensation for cancellation can sometimes improve both parties’ outcomes. Information and enforceability Even mutually profitable trades can fail if each side privately knows different information, cannot commit, or suspects the other will exploit a sunk investment. Observing a failed deal therefore does not alone prove the underlying project lacked value. Separate a negative total surplus from a difficulty dividing or verifying a positive one. Before treating a long-term contract as a solution, ask whether the promised quality, quantity and dates can be verified by someone independent. A detailed contract can increase negotiation costs and reduce flexibility. An analytical answer connects the proposed term to the exact point at which incentives otherwise diverge. title: Externalities and policy
detail: F02 · Lesson 10 · Microeconomics, Information and Financial Decisions
terms: A private return can omit costs borne by others. Apply the distinction to pollution or a bank whose failure disrupts payments for other firms. Private decisions and social costs A trucking company considers an extra delivery. The fee benefits the company and the production cost enters its accounts. Noise or congestion imposed on nearby residents can also be a consequence even when the company makes no payment for it. A cost or benefit borne by outsiders outside the price is an externality. To evaluate an additional unit, distinguish marginal private cost from marginal social cost. Social cost adds marginal external damage to the private resource cost. The efficient quantity equates marginal social benefit and marginal social cost under the usual assumptions. Average total damage divided by all units need not measure the extra harm caused by one more unit. Taxes, standards and bargaining A per-unit charge equal to marginal damage at the efficient quantity can make a privately maximizing supplier account for the external harm in a simple competitive model. A quantity standard directly limits production or pollution. The choice matters when damages, costs and enforcement differ among firms or are uncertain. Charging a tax transfers money to the government. When calculating total social surplus in this simple setting, subtract actual resource costs and damage. Do not subtract tax revenue again as a new loss. Distribution still matters because customers, suppliers and taxpayers may be affected differently. Monitoring or collection can create real costs if specified. Financial spillovers A bank can judge an exposure using its expected private return while overlooking disruption to borrowers and payment networks if it fails. This gives a finance example of potential external cost. Distinguish the bank’s own expected credit loss from a loss occurring elsewhere that was not already in its payoff calculation. A useful policy analysis asks what evidence would measure the additional spillover and what behaviour the intervention changes. A rule applied to one type of institution could move exposures elsewhere. A policy encouraging private precaution can still cost resources or reduce valuable lending, so assess both the external benefit and the real compliance or funding cost. title: Rates and units
detail: F03 · Lesson 1 · Financial Mathematics and the Time Value of Money
terms: A rise from 4% to 5% is one percentage point. Record the currency, sign, period and rate convention before calculating. A quote needs a clock and a base An annual interest quote of 6% can mean several different things. It might be a simple rate used to accrue interest over a stated fraction of a year, a nominal rate split into monthly periods, or an effective rate stating actual one-year growth. Before multiplying, state which interpretation the contract or question supplies. A basis point is 0.01 percentage points, or 0.0001 as a decimal rate. A move of 40 basis points changes a decimal rate by 0.004. A percentage change in the rate itself uses the old rate as the denominator. These calculations answer different questions even when printed as adjacent numbers. Time fractions in simple interest For simple interest, charge I = P × r × t, where P is outstanding principal, r is the decimal annual rate and t is the fraction of a year. If part of the principal is repaid during the period, split the interval into pieces with their own balances before calculating charges. Under an actual/360 convention, 30 actual days count as 30/360 years. Actual/365 fixed instead uses 30/365. This difference can matter on large balances. Other conventions exist. Use the stated convention and the actual accrual dates supplied, and avoid adding an unmentioned day at each end of the interval. Signs and currency in a timeline A borrower receives principal now and pays interest and principal later. A lender records the opposite signs at each date. Keeping one perspective prevents a supposed net benefit from appearing when both sides of the same transfer are accidentally added. Within one currency, interest has the same currency unit as principal. If a term sheet quotes a margin over a floating reference, add percentage points in matching units before multiplying. A 120-basis-point margin means 1.20 percentage points above the reference. A hypothetical change in annual rates does not affect an entire year’s expense when the quoted balance is outstanding for only part of that year. title: Compounding
detail: F03 · Lesson 2 · Financial Mathematics and the Time Value of Money
terms: Interest earns interest when it stays invested. Derive future value by multiplying by one plus the period rate for every period. From repeated growth to a product A savings balance consists of the initial deposit plus all interest left inside the account. After the first period the entire new balance earns the second period’s rate. Multiplication captures this reinvestment. Under simple interest, by contrast, each interest payment is calculated on the originally specified principal unless the contract sets a different base. Write each period as a growth factor 1 + r. This works for losses as well as gains as long as the price-return model remains meaningful. Rates of +20% and −20% have factors 1.20 and 0.80. Their product is 0.96, so an account can lose money even when the arithmetic average return is zero. A constant equivalent growth rate If a balance grows from P to F over n equal periods without deposits or withdrawals, a constant rate g satisfying P(1+g)ⁿ = F summarizes its realized path. Solving gives g = (F/P)^(1/n) − 1. This geometric average reproduces the actual endpoints when reinvested for n periods. An arithmetic average answers the average single-period rate among observations. It is useful for some forecasting questions but generally will not reconstruct a volatile realized path. The gap is economically important in comparing investment performance. A fund that receives external deposits presents an additional issue because those deposits can increase value without being an investment gain. When money enters halfway through Cash deposited between return periods earns only the returns after its deposit date. Draw a timeline and compound each contribution for its own number of periods. Do not compound a mid-year deposit for a full two years simply because the report covers two years. The order of returns affects the investor’s ending wealth when contributions or withdrawals occur. For the return on the investment strategy itself, one can break the timeline at external cash flows and combine the subperiod growth factors, if values are available around each flow. An investor-specific rate can instead reflect the timing and amount of that investor’s funds. Identify which question the performance comparison asks.
