title: Contract terms and payoff
detail: C07 · Lesson 1 · Derivatives and Risk Transfer
terms: Distinguish the cash paid today, future cash flows and profit after costs. Draw outcomes for the buyer and seller of the same contract. Read the contract as a set of rights Locate the underlying, the number of units, the price agreed in advance, the exercise or settlement date, and who can decide whether the exchange occurs. A forward obliges both sides to settle. A call lets its holder buy, and a put lets its holder sell, on the terms specified. Physical delivery transfers the underlying and requires funding or inventory. Cash settlement uses a defined price observation to calculate money owed. Even two contracts on oil can settle differently if their prices reference a different grade, location or day. Build a payoff one region at a time A forward buyer’s terminal payoff per unit is final spot minus delivery price. A call buyer receives the greater of zero and spot minus strike. A put buyer receives the greater of zero and strike minus spot. Each seller has the negative of the corresponding buyer payoff before considering premium or default. A premium paid upfront is a cash flow separate from the exercise payoff. To calculate profit at expiry, subtract the premium grown at the financing rate. Buying several legs produces a combined payoff by adding their signed, contract-sized amounts state by state. Interpret slope and limits The slope of a terminal payoff against spot price shows the additional cash received per unit price increase in that region. A protective put floors the gross terminal value of a share. Selling a call against the same share exchanges some upside for premium. A break-even is the usual point where total profit crosses zero. title: Forwards and carry

terms: Replicate later delivery by buying and financing the underlying today. Storage, dividends or other benefits of holding the asset affect fair delivery prices. Replicate delivery with a financed purchase A buyer wanting an asset on a future date can buy now and carry it or sign a forward for delivery later. If the two routes deliver identical cash flows and the asset can be freely bought, financed and sold, an executable price discrepancy can be traded against. Carry includes financing and cash costs, less benefits received by the holder. For a share paying known cash dividends before maturity, subtract the present value of dividends from spot before financing the remaining exposure. With discount factor d(T), fair delivery price is [spot − PV(dividends)]/d(T). Guaranteed storage charges add to costs under equivalent timing conventions. An existing forward can have value At inception a newly struck fair forward has zero value in the simple model. The delivery price printed on it remains fixed. Later market conditions can make that commitment advantageous. A long contract at old delivery price K has value d(t,T) × [current fair forward price − K] under matched settlement and credit assumptions. A favorable forward price difference is a terminal cash difference, so discount it to get value today. Distinguish the new forward quote, the old delivery price and the present market value required to transfer an existing contract. Find the correct arbitrage direction If market delivery is too dear relative to carrying the asset, borrow to buy the asset, retain relevant income and sell forward. At expiry deliver the asset and repay financing. If delivery is too cheap, reversing the strategy generally requires borrowing the physical asset and meeting its income obligations. A lower bound is the greater of zero and current share price minus the present value of the strike. For the corresponding put, the lower bound is the greater of zero and discounted strike minus share price. To understand a bound, compare terminal payoffs of the option with a traded portfolio that it dominates. If a portfolio can never pay more than the option, the portfolio cannot cost more under frictionless no-arbitrage. This logic avoids treating a pricing formula as a rule to memorize. Prove parity by matching every state One package buys a call and saves the discounted strike. The other buys one share and one put. If the final share price exceeds the strike, both deliver the share’s value. Below the strike, both deliver the strike. Thus call + PV(strike) = put + share for the matched European contracts without intervening dividends. If dividends are known, a holder of the share receives cash before expiry while the option package does not. terms: Match the option payoff in an up and a down state using shares and cash. The cost of the matching portfolio provides the model price. Solve two payoff equations At one node, let the underlying become Su or Sd next period and the derivative become Vu or Vd. Hold Δ shares and an amount B in cash today. At the next date cash grows by R. Match both states with ΔSu + BR = Vu and ΔSd + BR = Vd. Subtraction gives Δ = (Vu − Vd)/(Su − Sd). Then B = (Vd − ΔSd)/R. A negative B represents borrowing. The option’s present value is ΔS + B because the replicating portfolio behaves identically in both states. At the preceding nodes use local up and down option values to choose the local shares and cash. Once you have both intermediate values, repeat from the original node. title: Risk-neutral probability
detail: C07 · Lesson 7 · Derivatives and Risk Transfer
terms: Replication can be rewritten as a discounted expected payoff under pricing probabilities. These probabilities depend on traded prices and the financing rate. Derive the pricing weight from the share Let today’s share value be S and next-period outcomes Su and Sd. Choose q so discounting the weighted future share returns S today. The condition q × u + (1 − q) × d = R gives q = (R − d)/(u − d). When d < R < u the weight lies strictly between zero and one. This q prices every payoff replicable using the same share and safe asset under the model. It is an alternative notation for the two state prices q/R and (1 − q)/R. Pricing is therefore consistent across different securities that respond to identical modeled future states. Physical probability and priced probability An economist estimating how often shares rise provides a physical probability. A trader inferring q from observed prices provides the weight that values future cash consistently. The investor may demand a risk premium for holding shares, so the two weights can differ while today’s prices remain internally consistent. A real expected payoff computed with physical probabilities cannot generally be discounted at the safe rate for a risky claim. Doing so assumes away its priced risk. Conversely using q to forecast default frequency or to plan average sales can misstate actual expected outcomes. Extension to exercise decisions For a European option, backward induction at each node gives discounted risk-neutral next values. For an American-style option, compare that continuation value with current exercise value whenever exercise is permitted. Choose the larger because the holder decides. This can matter for puts or dividend-paying shares. Check the time unit in R. A 6% annual effective rate implies square-root growth over half a year, whereas a quoted simple six-month convention uses its own expression. Incorrect period funding changes both q and discounting. terms: Interpret volatility, delta, gamma and time decay. Continuous hedging and constant volatility are strong assumptions for a real desk. Black–Scholes as a replication model For a non-dividend-paying share with continuous price movements, geometric Brownian motion is a model in which short proportional changes have a random component scaled by volatility. Different strikes or dates can imply different volatilities, signalling limitations of a single constant-volatility assumption or different priced risks. detail: C07 · Lesson 9 · Derivatives and Risk Transfer
terms: Exchange fixed for floating cash flows on a notional amount. The initial fair fixed rate makes the two legs equal in value under stated curves. Translate the swap into dated legs A fixed-for-floating swap makes one side pay a fixed rate and receive a reference floating rate, typically on the same notional in a plain single-currency contract. Payment on a period equals rate × notional × accrual fraction. Netting the two interest payments does not remove the economic exposure to either leg. The floating rate may reset in advance or accrue in arrears under the reference convention. A period that has already reset has a known contractual payment, while later periods require projected rates. Include any accrued amount in a mark-to-market measured between payment dates. Derive a par fixed rate Let A be the sum of each fixed-leg accrual fraction multiplied by its payment discount factor. A fixed coupon K on notional N has present value NKA. Project each floating cash flow under its appropriate forward convention and discount it. At inception the fixed rate that equates these leg values is the par swap rate. In a simple single-curve swap beginning today on reset with no spread and matching conventions, floating-leg value excluding principal is N × [1 − d(T)]. In a multi-curve setting, project coupons and discount them with their respective curves. The compact identity may no longer apply. Why an old swap moves in value The fixed rate in an existing contract stays fixed. If comparable market fixed rates rise, a party paying the older lower fixed rate generally benefits, all else equal. A swap’s value is a signed difference in present leg values rather than the notional exchanged. To hedge floating-rate borrowing, a company typically pays fixed and receives floating over matching dates. A loan margin over the reference rate remains. title: Clearing and counterparty risk
detail: C07 · Lesson 10 · Derivatives and Risk Transfer
terms: Collateral and clearing change loss and funding exposures. Assess the chosen hedge after fees, margin needs and possible failure of the counterparty. Replacement cost and the netting set A firm facing a defaulted counterparty may need to replace contracts at current market prices. A positive replacement value is a claim. An enforceable closeout netting agreement may allow assets and liabilities with the same counterparty and legal set to offset before calculating that claim. Separate agreements or entities may not be eligible to net. Collateral received can reduce unsecured exposure to the extent it is legally available, correctly valued and liquid. Apply any contractual haircut to collateral value. Posted collateral has a different role from collateral received and can create a claim for its return under the arrangement. Current and potential future exposure Current exposure uses today’s positive replacement value after qualifying netting and collateral. Potential future exposure asks how large it might become over a future interval. During the margin period of risk, prices can change between the last margin call and completed closeout. A fully margined portfolio today can therefore produce a loss after a jump. Wrong-way risk arises if exposure grows precisely when the counterparty is likely to fail or its collateral becomes less valuable. A hedge for oil purchases bought from an oil-dependent distressed counterparty can display this dependence. Scenario modeling should join default, trade value and collateral. What central clearing changes A clearinghouse interposes itself between counterparties for eligible trades. Clearing members post margin and contribute to loss-absorbing resources under a stated waterfall. Variation margin addresses accumulated price changes. Initial margin provides a buffer for potential changes during closeout. Default arrangements and contributions depend on the clearinghouse rules. Netting and collateral can reduce exposures yet concentrate operational and liquidity needs. A firm may have to post cash on a cleared hedge before its underlying receipt arrives. title: Why intermediaries exist
detail: C08 · Lesson 1 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: A bank can reduce the cost of screening and monitoring many borrowers on behalf of many small savers. Identify the friction a bank addresses In a direct financing market, a borrower could issue a claim to savers. That works more readily when public information is reliable, the issue is large enough to justify disclosure, and investors can sell or diversify cheaply. Small opaque businesses may face high costs proving their prospects to many separate lenders. A bank can screen applications before lending, write a contract that allocates risks, and follow up when outcomes disappoint. Screening concerns information before the contract. Monitoring concerns information and behaviour after it. These functions can be valuable even when the bank also supplies payments and deposits. Economies of scale and relationship information One institution can spread the fixed cost of an industry analyst or underwriting system across many loans. Repeated interaction may reveal seasonal customer payments or management quality unavailable in a public report. Relationship-specific information can help a viable borrower obtain credit during a temporary difficulty. The same informational advantage can give a lender bargaining power if competitors cannot verify the borrower cheaply. An established relationship can also encourage delaying recognition of a bad loan. Ask whether the intermediary produces information, how it uses it and what incentives discipline the decision. Compare technology, risk bearing and alternatives Intermediation can also transform maturity, manage liquidity and diversify independent exposures. A transaction platform reducing search costs need not perform borrower monitoring, and a mutual fund holding public bonds need not promise demand deposits. Identify the precise contract behind an institution’s service. Changing technology can lower direct distribution and screening costs, changing which route is efficient. A firm could move from bank funding toward public bonds as it grows. There is no fixed size threshold independent of information, scale and market access. title: The bank balance sheet
detail: C08 · Lesson 2 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Loans and cash are assets. Deposits and other borrowing are liabilities. Equity absorbs losses before creditors under the simplified priority model. Follow a loss through the balance sheet The balance sheet is a snapshot of what the bank controls and owes. Loans are assets because customers owe the bank. Deposits are liabilities because the bank promises funds to depositors. Equity is the residual claim left after liabilities. Expenses and credit losses generally reduce income and, other things equal, retained earnings and equity. A deposit withdrawal reduces cash and a deposit liability together, with no mechanical equity loss if the bank can meet it at recorded value. A discounted forced sale used to fund the withdrawal can generate a separate loss. Post each transaction before combining their effects. Leverage and asymmetric outcomes Assets divided by equity is a simple leverage measure. If a bank has €20 of assets per €1 of equity, an unanticipated 1% asset loss consumes 20% of starting equity if liabilities are fixed. Ownership returns respond to the spread earned across a much larger asset base. Debtholders can still be exposed if losses exceed equity. Book equity uses recognized accounting figures. Economic equity values assets and liabilities at an appropriate valuation convention and can diverge, especially when market yields or expected credit losses change. Label the basis before comparing cushions or calculating a threshold. Risk weights and regulatory concepts A raw equity-to-assets ratio gives equal weight to each asset euro. A simplified risk-weighted measure assigns different weights to specified categories and compares eligible capital with weighted assets. The eligible numerator can differ from ordinary book equity and regulations vary by jurisdiction. Use classroom weights only when explicitly supplied. A bank can shrink a ratio’s denominator without adding much equity, for example by replacing a high-weight asset with a lower-weight one. This improves the quoted ratio under the assumed rules but may still leave interest-rate or liquidity exposure. Inspect both numerator and underlying economic risk. title: Deposit creation and settlement
detail: C08 · Lesson 3 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Making a loan can create a matching deposit. Payment to another bank can create a need for reserves or wholesale funding. Record loan origination at one institution A bank accepting a borrower’s signed promise can credit a deposit to that borrower. The bank records a loan asset and an equal deposit liability. The deposit becomes spendable. The transaction expands the bank’s balance sheet, but creates no new equity and no new central-bank reserves on its own. New bank deposits are a form of money for their holders. Central-bank reserves are an asset of eligible institutions used for settlement. A household’s deposit and a bank’s reserve balance are claims on different entities. Treating the two balances as interchangeable obscures who can pay whom. Clear and settle a customer’s payment When a payment goes to another bank, the receiving institution credits its customer and obtains settlement funds, subject to payment-system arrangements. Netting can reduce gross reserve transfers if opposing customer payments occur. A transfer between customers of one bank generally changes the names on its deposit accounts only. The originating bank may meet outflows using reserves, receiving incoming payments, selling assets or borrowing against collateral. Constraints on funding, profitable lending opportunities, credit risk, capital and regulation affect its ability and willingness to expand. A fixed reserve multiplier misses these decisions. Reverse the entries at principal repayment A borrower paying principal from a deposit at the lending bank reduces both the bank’s loan asset and its deposit liability. If the borrower pays from another bank, settlement moves reserves as well. Principal repayment can reduce system-wide deposit money under these simplified assumptions. Interest income and government or central-bank transactions need separate entries. A default write-off instead reduces the bank’s loan and equity or previously recognized allowances. A deposit created long ago may now be held by a completely different person at another bank. Losing the loan does not automatically reverse that person’s deposit. title: Delegated monitoring
detail: C08 · Lesson 4 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Diversification can reduce the cost of delegating borrower oversight. Ask who monitors the intermediary and how the contract gives it incentives. Separate monitoring from the promise to savers A borrower may know project cash flow or effort better than outside funders. If every small saver must verify what happened before being paid, monitoring is duplicated and some may free-ride on others. A bank can act on their behalf and issue savers a simpler claim on its collective assets. Delegation introduces a second information problem. Savers cannot cheaply observe every monitoring decision the bank makes. The intermediary’s contract, own stake, reputation and institutional oversight help give it incentives. The theory asks whether savings from delegation exceed these extra costs. Why diversification helps this mechanism If many monitored borrowers have independent project outcomes, total collections can become more predictable relative to their average. A bank funded by debt may then meet relatively simple promises to savers across most outcomes even when individual borrower outcomes are difficult to verify. Diversifying a portfolio does not reduce its arithmetic expected credit loss merely by itself. It can reduce the risk of many defaults at once and the expected agency cost associated with the intermediary failing to meet its own obligations. Common shocks slow or eliminate that pooling benefit. Test whether monitoring is worth the effort A monitor incurs a cost whether or not a problem is ultimately found. Its benefit can come from preventing misuse, improving recovery, renegotiating promptly or distinguishing a sound firm from a weak one. Some benefit accrues to creditors, some to shareholders and potentially some to new lenders or the borrower. A bank chooses effort based on the share of improvement it captures, not necessarily the full social benefit. Selling most of a loan while keeping little loss exposure can reduce monitoring incentives unless contracts retain risk, pay for verifiable actions or impose consequences for poor servicing. title: Liquidity insurance
detail: C08 · Lesson 5 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Depositors value the ability to withdraw early. A bank can offer this while holding longer-lived assets if withdrawals are sufficiently predictable. A two-date economy with uncertain needs Households may discover early that they need cash immediately, while others can wait and benefit from a productive long-term project. Each household initially faces the risk of becoming an early spender. Holding only liquid cash sacrifices some return. Investing everything long risks an expensive premature sale. A bank can pool such liquidity risks. If the share of early customers is predictable in aggregate, it can hold liquid resources for their withdrawals and invest the rest long. Depositors value a redeemable claim partly because their spending date is uncertain before they invest. Choose a feasible deposit promise Suppose n customers each deposit one unit. If a fraction λ needs an early payment c₁, the bank requires nλc₁ liquid units at the early date. Long assets that survive pay R later and can fund c₂ for the remaining customers. Write both resource constraints before judging generosity. The feasible contract may redistribute across early and late types. Preferences over consumption timing and risk determine whether an allocation is desirable. Liquidity insurance is about pooling timing shocks. Simply maximizing expected asset return can leave early customers unable to consume when needed. When pooled demand becomes correlated A common emergency, loss of confidence or the disappearance of an expected funding line can produce more early withdrawals than the designed buffer covers. Liquidating long assets at a discount reduces what remains for later customers. The early promise becomes fragile when others can also choose to withdraw. A larger liquid reserve reduces forced sales but uses funds that could have produced a higher late return. Committed liquidity, deposit maturity and redemption rules also influence this trade-off. Test whether support remains available under the same common event that increases withdrawals. Check a deposit contract A pooled contract and a surprise withdrawal

title: Runs and coordination
detail: C08 · Lesson 6 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: If customers expect others to withdraw, early withdrawal can become individually attractive. Model an otherwise viable bank facing forced sales. Withdrawal decisions can reinforce each other Consider a bank that promises early payment to customers on demand and holds long assets that pay well if allowed to mature. A patient saver may value a late claim more than an early one when few others withdraw. The same saver may rationally prefer to move early when a large queue would exhaust liquid resources. This is strategic complementarity. One customer’s reason to withdraw strengthens when others do. A run can therefore reflect a coordination failure even without newly discovered bad loans. There can also be a run driven by genuine insolvency. The observable queue alone does not distinguish these mechanisms. Why first-come service matters If a bank pays early claimants at par until funds run out, position in the queue matters. Selling long assets for less than their maturity value shrinks the resources left for those who wait. An expectation of widespread withdrawals can become self-fulfilling under an otherwise viable contract. The result depends on rules. Credible deposit protection, payment suspension provisions or reliable collateralized liquidity can change incentives and timing. Their costs and scope matter, including possible hardship for households with genuine early needs. A classroom model can specify them explicitly without assuming identical rules everywhere. Distinguish fire sales from fundamental losses Compare going-concern asset value with total obligations, then compare immediate cash and forced-sale value with runnable claims. A bank can pass the first and fail the second. If underlying asset payments themselves are also too small, removing the queue cannot restore long-run solvency. Depositors and potential emergency lenders often lack reliable information about which situation applies. A fall in collateral market prices can simultaneously reduce emergency funding and affect confidence. Test both a liquidity-only and an underlying-credit-loss scenario. title: Interest margins
detail: C08 · Lesson 7 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Income on assets and funding costs reprice at different speeds. Higher market rates can help or hurt earnings depending on the bank’s exposures. Two measures of rate exposure Net interest income measures currency interest received on assets less paid on liabilities over an interval. Net interest margin divides it by average interest-earning assets. Economic value of equity instead asks how the present values of assets and liabilities change. Rising rates can improve short-term income while damaging the economic value of longer assets. A fixed-rate loan pays its old coupon until maturity or reset. A floating-rate loan can reprice at a contractual fixing. Deposits may reprice by a fraction of the market move, called deposit beta in this context. Deposit beta is a funding pass-through parameter, distinct from equity-market beta. Repricing gaps and deposit behaviour A simple repricing gap subtracts rate-sensitive liabilities from rate-sensitive assets assigned to a time bucket. Multiplying the gap by the rate movement approximates income change if all bucket members reset promptly by the same amount. Partial pass-through, different reset dates, floors and caps break that shortcut. A bank may gain initially by keeping deposit rates low, then lose customers to money-market funds and have to replace cheap balances with wholesale funding. Forecast volumes, competitive pricing and funding stability as well as the mechanical rate shock. Check contracts and hedges A borrower’s contractual margin can compensate credit and administrative costs. It is distinct from the market reference rate. When reference rates fall below a contractual floor, a floating loan may respond asymmetrically. Swaps can shift repricing exposure but bring collateral, basis and counterparty effects. Measure over a clearly stated horizon. A six-month repricing lag alters interest for only part of the first year, even if it changes the full following year. Average earning assets in the denominator may themselves change if funding leaves or loans run off. Forecast a margin bridge Deposits reprice sooner than loans

title: Capital versus liquidity
detail: C08 · Lesson 8 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Insolvency concerns the value of assets relative to liabilities. Illiquidity concerns the cash available to meet obligations when due. Three questions on one balance sheet Solvency asks whether asset value covers liabilities under a stated valuation basis. Liquidity asks whether obligations can be settled when due. Regulatory capital compares eligible loss-absorbing resources with a specified measure of exposures. A bank can pass one or two tests and fail another. Cash is an asset, while equity is a residual source of finance. Selling an asset at its carrying value converts one asset into another, usually improving immediately accessible cash without increasing equity. Selling below carrying value also realizes a loss and can damage capital. Build a dated liquidity ladder List opening unencumbered cash, reliable inflows, unavoidable outflows and available actions by time bucket. Exclude collateral already pledged unless genuinely reusable. An asset’s gross market value overstates cash that can be borrowed against it if a haircut applies. The same asset cannot be simultaneously sold and pledged. A liquidity ratio gives a useful summary only for the time period, outflow assumptions and eligible resources in its definition. A large obligation due in one hour can bind before next-day receipts arrive. Stress both volume and timing under a common scenario. Fire sales can transmit illiquidity into insolvency If a bank needs cash G and assets sell for a fraction h of carrying value, it must sell G/h of book assets. Realized loss is G/h − G. Compare that loss with actual equity capacity. An initially solvent bank can lose its capital by meeting a large sudden withdrawal through deep discounts. Collateralized borrowing can avoid immediate sale losses but creates a new liability and a claim on pledged assets. It can buy time for solvent cash flows to mature. If underlying asset losses remain large, borrowing alone cannot create the equity needed to absorb them. Run a liquidity and capital stress A sale clears payments but uses capital

title: Supervision and safety nets
detail: C08 · Lesson 9 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Deposit protection, lender-of-last-resort facilities and capital rules can stabilize funding while also changing incentives to take risks. Match the instrument to the failure Deposit protection changes the payoff to eligible depositors if a bank fails, potentially weakening the incentive to run. It need not make the bank’s assets whole. Emergency liquidity can deliver settlement cash against acceptable collateral. Capital requirements and new capital address capacity to absorb losses. A resolution process deals with a failing institution, continuity of important functions and allocation of losses under applicable law. Classroom cases should specify which claims are protected and which can bear losses. Coverage limits, central-bank eligibility and lender terms are institutional facts, not universal constants. Incentives created by a safety net When depositors believe they will be repaid regardless of bank risk, they may demand less compensation or monitor management less. Shareholders with limited downside can then profit from risky lending at the expense of a guarantee fund if safeguards are weak. This is a moral-hazard channel. Risk-sensitive premiums, credible supervision, limits on risk exposure, loss-absorbing equity and orderly resolution can address different dimensions of that incentive. An excessively costly or stigmatized facility might discourage a solvent institution from seeking liquidity when early use would help. Asset haircuts and institutional feasibility A lender providing emergency cash needs to verify eligible collateral, ownership, legal documentation, valuation and operational readiness. A 20% haircut on collateral worth €10m permits at most €8m borrowing on that asset under the stated simple rule. Amount and date of access matter as much as headline eligibility. A guarantee can reduce a run without disbursing funds immediately if depositors trust its coverage and payout process. Delays may still matter to households with urgent expenses. A capital injection can increase both cash and equity if paid in cash, though who provides it and at what price affect ownership. Evaluate an intervention Haircuts and a residual capital hole

title: Cross-border banking
detail: C08 · Lesson 10 · Banking and Financial Intermediation
terms: Branches, subsidiaries, currency mismatches and uneven access to group funding change where a shock is absorbed. Trace the legal entity that owes the cash. Locate the relevant legal balance sheet A foreign branch is part of its parent bank’s legal entity. A subsidiary is a separately incorporated institution with its own assets, liabilities and usually its own local obligations. Both can appear in a consolidated report, but the legal identity of the payer affects collateral access, claim priority and the feasibility of intragroup transfers. A parent guarantee is a specific contingent contract. Common branding or common ownership alone does not establish one. Even when a parent promises support, verify trigger, currency, enforceability and the time at which cash can reach the subsidiary. A group aggregate can hide currency risk A subsidiary lending long in local currency and funding short in dollars can be exposed both to exchange-rate losses and to dollar refinancing. A currency swap may reduce valuation sensitivity. Its rollover, counterparty exposure and collateral calls can still generate dollar funding needs at inconvenient dates. Net open currency position is different from same-day currency liquidity. Dollar assets due next year can match a dollar liability’s amount while providing nothing for a dollar payment due today. Construct separate cash ladders by currency and legal entity. Examine cross-border transmission A group treasury under stress might call intercompany balances or refuse to roll a line, transmitting stress to a locally sound business. Conversely, local restrictions can prevent a healthy subsidiary’s cash from supporting the parent. Operating profits consolidated into group reports can be trapped at a particular entity. Home and host authorities may have different priorities and laws. Use specified transfer assumptions in exercises. Distinguish facts about binding restrictions from simulated stress measures or unconfirmed management intentions before judging the ability to meet foreign obligations. title: The market for corporate control
detail: S01 · Lesson 1 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Study horizontal, vertical and diversifying acquisitions. Ownership changes can improve control of assets, but the existence of a bidder does not establish an efficiency gain. Who controls an asset? A contract can buy a service without buying the company that supplies it. Owning the supplier gives the buyer authority over decisions the contract did not anticipate. A roaster and a coffee grower, for example, can agree on a price today without agreeing exactly how to respond to a poor harvest next year. The value of ownership depends on what that additional authority makes possible. One owner can coordinate an investment both parties previously feared the other might exploit. It can also weaken incentives if the grower now bears less responsibility for quality. Examine both the proposed improvement and what independent ownership did well. Why a takeover market exists If shares can be bought and control transferred, an outsider can profit by replacing weak management or redeploying idle assets. The threat of replacement can itself influence managers. Yet control is expensive to acquire. Costs of identifying a change, paying advisers and carrying it out reduce the prize. Horizontal deals combine rivals, vertical deals connect stages of production, and diversifying deals join different businesses. These are descriptions of the relationship, not predictions of gain. Two rivals might consolidate empty production lines or gain bargaining power to raise prices. These produce very different outcomes for customers. How much of the change benefits society? A cost saving releases resources that can serve other uses. A rise in profit paid for entirely by customers through higher prices can transfer wealth even if the same quantities of labour, materials and capital are used. Positive shareholder gains alone cannot settle whether customers, suppliers or employees benefited from the transaction. Spell out the comparison. The relevant alternative may be a long-term supply contract or a joint venture, rather than business as usual. If a contract can produce the same coordination at lower cost, willingness to pay for full control should reflect the smaller incremental advantage. Compare three ownership arrangements The glass supply decision

title: Competing merger theories
detail: S01 · Lesson 2 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Contrast scale economies, market power, managerial empire building, overconfidence and misvaluation. Derive a prediction each explanation makes about the target, payment or outcome. Build a claim that could be wrong A merger story is useful when it predicts something distinct from rival explanations. Economies of scale mean average resource cost falls as the business grows. A producer operating two partially used factories could close one and produce the same units with fewer fixed overheads. Market power means the business gains an ability to improve its terms against customers or suppliers. Reported margins can rise in either story. Compare physical inputs per unit, output, prices relative to rivals and geographic overlap to learn which explanation the observations fit. Whose objective drives the bid? Shareholders might seek a gain on their invested capital while a manager values a larger budget, prestige or compensation. This conflict is called an agency problem. A manager acting in good faith can also overestimate likely benefits. Both motives can produce overpayment, but their predictions differ. Overconfidence suggests optimistic forecasts and weak allowance for failure. Empire building suggests expansion despite weak forecasts, particularly when pay or status depends on size. A stock-financed purchase could also reflect perceived mispricing or a desire to share combined risk. One financing choice rarely identifies the motive by itself. How to use evidence fairly Write the prediction before looking at the result. Test it against credible alternatives and ask what would change your mind. A fall in cost per unit during a general decline in energy prices does not automatically establish useful plant consolidation. Different explanations can coexist. Paying a defensible price for genuine production savings can still leave customers worse off through reduced competition. An analyst should say which evidence supports each part and name an observation that carries little weight because several theories predict it. title: Standalone value and control
detail: S01 · Lesson 3 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Value the target before combining it with the buyer. Separate improvements available to any new controller from gains available only to this particular combination. Value three different versions of the company Start with cash the target can distribute under its current policies. Next value it under realistic changes any capable owner could make. Finally estimate extra cash requiring this particular buyer’s technology, distribution or assets. Give each improvement a home in exactly one version. Control value is the difference between the first two valuations when control enables the improvements. The economic gain is the change in cash or risk, not the appearance of the word control in the agreement. If current managers are already implementing the changes, their benefit belongs in the original forecast. Connect forecasts to the type of claim A value based on cash available to shareholders is an equity value. A value based on operations before financing is an enterprise value. Compare a proposed share purchase with equity value. To use operating value, adjust for debt, eligible cash and other claims consistently. One common shortcut multiplies a target’s share price by a historical control premium. It conceals why a premium might exist and can double count expectations already priced by the market. A concrete forecast identifies which changes are achievable, who can implement them and why a competitor might value the target differently. Competing bidders set the bargaining range A buyer-specific ceiling is the highest price leaving that buyer with zero gain under its assumptions. A rival with fewer unique benefits may still bid strongly for improvements available to everybody. A seller’s alternatives affect the likely price between the competing valuations. The greatest theoretical improvement is rarely a certainty. A turnaround may depend on labour agreements, capital expenditure or time. Probability-weight the distinct outcomes or model risk consistently in the discounting. Do not count a saving as certain and then omit the conditions for achieving it. title: Synergies and implementation costs
detail: S01 · Lesson 4 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Forecast incremental cash, timing, tax, investment and integration costs. Discount uncertain cost savings or revenue gains once and document overlap with standalone improvements. Forecast the change in cash A duplicate distribution centre looks like a cost saving until somebody asks whether its lease can end. Translate each proposed benefit into a physical action, its earliest date and the cash cost that genuinely disappears. An accounting allocation that moves to the surviving site does not disappear from group cash. Revenue gains need a margin calculation. Selling €1m of extra goods may add only €0.2m after production, distribution and service. A new sale to a customer who would otherwise buy a different group product may create even less. Compare the combined plan with both firms’ standalone plans. Distinguish the timetable from the annual target Managers often quote a run rate, meaning a full year’s saving once the changes are complete. A €4m run rate at the end of year two does not imply €4m in each of the first two years. Plot the ramp-up, tax, extra investment and any cash needed for inventories and customer credit. Discount the cash flows using rates consistent with their currencies and risks. If the forecasts already include the probability that an uncertain benefit fails, avoid an unexplained second haircut for the same outcome. Prepare at least one coherent delayed or reduced-benefit scenario. What can be added together? Positive savings and negative effects may share the same cause. Closing a store might save rent while losing some customers whose nearest branch is now farther away. Forecast them together. A contract binding the group to pay rent until year three changes the timing of the saving again. Assign responsibility for each driver and compare overlapping proposals. Procurement discounts can reduce the cost base used in a factory-closure estimate. Adding both savings using the original cost base would count some costs twice. Multiple spreadsheets require one consolidated cash-flow bridge. Price an integration plan A two-year procurement arrangement

title: Premiums and bargaining
detail: S01 · Lesson 5 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: The unaffected share price, standalone fundamental value and negotiated offer can differ. Explain which reference price measures a market premium and which one supports a reservation price. Choose the right starting price The market premium answers how much the offer exceeds a chosen traded price. A price observed before credible takeover rumours is often useful because trading after the leak may already reflect the expected deal. Record the date used, changes in the broader market and other news affecting comparisons. Standalone fundamental value answers a different question. It estimates future cash if the company remains independent. It can differ from the historic share price or from what a seller expects to receive by waiting. A premium over market price does not by itself measure the total value created. Identify each party’s alternative A reservation price is the worst transaction a party would accept given its next best alternative. A seller may have a competing bid, or may prefer to remain independent. A buyer might build a plant itself. Each outside option narrows the range in which both parties gain. If a buyer can produce a gain of €9m through acquisition but can earn €4m on an equally feasible mutually exclusive alternative, it can give up at most €5m beyond standalone value before preferring the alternative. Other constraints, including financing or approval, can narrow the feasible range further. Who captures the surplus? In a simple cash acquisition, seller gain equals price minus standalone target value. Incremental buyer gain from the combination equals net synergy less that premium. One can also compare each party with its outside option. State which comparison is being made before labelling a surplus or loss. Negotiating strength relates to credible alternatives and time pressure. If several bidders can generate the same improvement, competition can transfer much of it to the seller. An auction result can reflect optimistic projections too. A winner should examine the possibility that it made the most generous error. title: Cash, shares and exchange ratios
detail: S01 · Lesson 6 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: A cash offer fixes nominal consideration. A share offer gives sellers a stake in the combined firm, so the exchange ratio distributes future gains and losses. Cash changes who bears the risk With an all-cash offer, sellers know the agreed nominal amount if the deal completes. The remaining buyers bear changes in combined value after that point. Financing the cash may expose the buyer to interest, refinancing or leverage risk. A signed agreement can still have completion conditions. In a fixed-ratio share exchange, sellers receive a specified number of buyer shares per target share. This puts them on both sides of the merger’s future economics. If integration goes badly their shares can lose value even though the agreed exchange ratio never changes. From exchange ratio to economic ownership Multiply the number of target shares by the ratio to find new shares. Then divide the new shares by all shares after the issue. An exchange ratio of 0.5 describes a transfer per target share. It says nothing about sellers’ ownership without both firms’ original share counts. After combining, value per share equals combined equity value divided by all shares, assuming identical ordinary shares and no other changes. The seller’s realized consideration is new shares times that price. Multiplying new shares by the old bidder price instead gives an announcement reference amount, which may differ. What happens at the boundaries? A fixed-value share offer aims to deliver a set value and may calculate the share count using a specified pricing period. A collar limits the protection or share adjustment outside agreed boundaries. Read exactly whose downside is limited, when the reference is measured and what happens when the limit binds. For a simple fixed-ratio offer, calculate seller value under multiple combined values. Compare buyer owners’ retained stake with their original equity. Sellers may accept a lower cash equivalent today if they expect greater upside than the buyer, or may demand cash to avoid concentration in one company. Reconstruct the post-deal register A fixed exchange between two distributors

title: Financing and earnings per share
detail: S01 · Lesson 7 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Build sources and uses, shares issued and interest expense. A deal can raise earnings per share while destroying value if the buyer pays too much. A share is a fraction of the profits Earnings per share divides profit available to ordinary owners by the relevant number of shares. For a simple full-year pro forma comparison, add target earnings, subtract new financing costs after any stated tax effect, include forecast changes to earnings and divide by the post-deal count. State if a partial year or diluted share count is required. An accretive deal raises earnings per share. A dilutive one lowers it. The arithmetic responds to the earnings yield of the acquired firm, the price of debt or newly issued shares and accounting charges. It says little about the duration or risk of those earnings. Why price and accounting profit can disagree A buyer with highly valued shares can exchange a small number for a company whose profits trade cheaply. Even with unchanged combined operating cash, earnings per share may rise. Existing holders still lose if they surrender a larger fraction of combined economic value than the acquired assets contribute. Debt funding can produce a similar illusion. Interest may be low this year while principal remains due later. The purchase price is exchanged for an asset and does not pass through current earnings as an immediate expense. To test value, model the cash available to investors relative to what they paid. Keep the funding table separate List uses such as purchase consideration, refinancing and fees against debt, cash on hand and any new equity. Cash drawn from the buyer’s balance sheet also has an opportunity cost. Consistently distinguish recurring interest and recurring operating profit from one-time integration expenses. A credible comparison reports assumptions about tax deductibility, share issue dates and any acquisition-accounting charges. A temporary EPS increase can reverse once a teaser loan rate resets or a new asset is depreciated. Look at the profile across several years before interpreting an earnings metric. Compute two different answers A cash bid at cheap funding

detail: S01 · Lesson 8 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Challenge earnings quality, net debt and normal working capital. Identify which conclusion changes price, which changes contractual protection and which makes the buyer walk away. Follow a deal assumption back to evidence A diligence team does more than collect statements. It tests assertions that make a bid work. A forecast may assume a customer will renew for three years. A contract can establish cancellation rights. Payment records can establish past behaviour. Neither alone proves that future demand will continue. Classify a finding by its economic effect. Recurring operating weakness reduces projected earnings. An existing unpaid obligation may reduce the payment for shares at closing. A contingent dispute may call for a defined contractual remedy, scenario valuation or withdrawal. Different categories require different evidence and arithmetic. Build the price bridge Operating value gives the price of the business before allocating claims between lenders and shareholders. In a simple deal, equity proceeds equal operating value plus eligible cash less agreed net debt items, plus or minus working-capital departures from an agreed normal balance. The signed definitions govern the calculation. Keep a single issue register to prevent double counting. A pre-closing claim could already have reduced both current profit and the value forecast. Reviewing historic profit, assessing future profitability and counting a legal obligation are distinct questions. State which cash effect each adjustment represents. Decide whether a contract actually protects the buyer An indemnity can assign the cost of a specified event to the seller if it occurs. Its economic value depends on scope, limits, time limits and whether the seller can still pay. It does not cure a permanently declining customer base. Evidence of lost repeat business generally requires a forecast revision. The most important finding need not be the largest booked figure. A missing operating licence or unreliable sales records may make valuation impossible over a wide range. title: Deal process and control contests
detail: S01 · Lesson 9 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Compare negotiated mergers, tender offers and auctions. Evaluate takeover defences and incentives of boards, managers, bidders and minority owners under the stated case rules. How the sale process changes the outcome In a negotiated transaction a bidder can learn about the business before fixing its price and tailor contractual protections. An auction may create competition and reveal alternatives, but limits time for investigation and can raise the risk of winning on overoptimistic assumptions. A tender offer asks owners directly to sell under specified conditions. Control rights and board procedures vary across jurisdictions. Reconstruct the rules stated for a case, including acceptance thresholds, approvals, voting eligibility and the treatment of remaining owners. A bidder owning a large minority can influence a company without having the automatic power to implement every desired action. Compare conditional offers on one date Shareholders care about payment if an offer closes, what remains if it fails, timing and any costs. A price conditional on financing is not equivalent to the same amount in cash today. Compute an expected outcome under stated probabilities, then discount any later outcome to a common date. An expected value is not a guaranteed payment. Shareholders with liquidity needs or concentrated holdings may value certainty differently. A board can ask a bidder for a committed financing package or clearer conditions to address completion risk, instead of arguing about headline price alone. Whose incentives shape a defence? A defence might give a board time to solicit a stronger competing bid or protect management from replacement. Examine the governance process, independent advice, treatment of minority shareholders and realistic alternative offers. Delay has an opportunity cost if the original bid can expire. A rival’s intervention can increase the target’s bargaining power but reduce expected value to the original bidder. Separately evaluate buyer and seller decisions. A bid that maximizes the target’s expected outcome may exceed the original buyer’s reservation price. Evaluate two offers A tender with a financing condition

title: Cross-border execution
detail: S01 · Lesson 10 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Currency, regulatory review, tax structure and ownership approvals affect timing and completion risk. Model delay and failure separately from operating synergy. The offer and the funding use different currencies A target’s owners can demand a fixed amount in their currency while the bidder manages a home-currency cash budget. Specify the quotation convention before converting. At 20 local units per euro, divide the amount of local currency by 20 to get euros. Strengthening of the local currency makes the purchase more expensive in euros. Price exposure between signing and closing is different from the operating currency exposure after an acquisition. A hedge against the purchase price may protect a funding limit while doing nothing to protect future foreign revenues. Evaluate the two separately so that cash needed at close remains visible. Treat completion and delay as different states Regulatory approval, counterparty financing or contract conditions can determine whether and when the purchase completes. Under a delay, the asset may still arrive while a forward contract matures earlier. Under failure the company needs no target currency but may still owe a settlement on the hedge. A binding forward fixes an exchange rate. A purchased currency option can give the bidder the choice to exchange while charging a premium. The right response depends on likelihood of completion, size of the exposure, funding flexibility and the value of certainty. A forward’s zero initial premium is not zero economic risk. Keep tax and regulation tied to the case Group cash cannot always be transferred freely. A locally earned cash stream and cash accessible to the buyer may differ after stipulated withholding or repatriation restrictions. Record the date, currency, tax base and who bears the tax before deducting it. Real transactions need the applicable local rules. Transactions can face approval conditions that weaken the very source of synergy. A requirement to sell part of the combined operation might reduce the benefit even when the deal closes. title: Empirical merger research
detail: S01 · Lesson 11 · Mergers and Acquisitions
terms: Estimate abnormal returns around an announcement and combine gains using pre-event equity values. Discuss anticipation, competing news and selection of completed deals. Measure the surprise in a share price Prices reflect information investors already expect. An event study asks whether a share’s return around new information differed from a reasonable estimate of its normal return. With a simple market model, expected return is an intercept plus sensitivity to the market times the market return, estimated before the event. An abnormal return is actual return minus that benchmark. A cumulative abnormal return adds abnormal returns across a short event window. Define trading dates in each market and the timing of the announcement. News published after an exchange closes may be reflected in its next trading session. Weight gains by the money exposed A 10% target increase and a 2% bidder loss cannot be compared until their original equity values are known. Multiply each abnormal return by its own pre-event value, add those amounts and divide by their combined initial equity if a combined percentage is needed. The combined reaction is an estimate of investors’ revisions to shareholder value around the announcement. It can include valuation news about the bidder, changing completion expectations or a revelation that the target had other interested buyers. It cannot establish realized operating cash flows several years later. Design choices that can reverse a conclusion A short window reduces unrelated news but may miss rumours or delayed trading. A longer window catches more deal-related anticipation and more unrelated earnings or policy shocks. Prepare a timeline and inspect alternative reasonable windows. Select the primary specification before seeing which produces the largest result. A sample limited to deals that eventually close describes a selected population. Abandoned deals also appeared in investors’ information at announcement. A historical average with statistical uncertainty does not tell what every firm gained or whether one country’s takeover institutions generalize elsewhere. terms: Compare realized savings and standalone trends with the pre-deal case. Build a counterfactual for what would likely have happened without the transaction. Set up a fair post-deal comparison A deal forecast is a frozen record of what the buyer believed at signing. A realized income statement is the result of both integration and everything else that happened. Separate the comparison with the original business case from the causal question of what would have occurred without the merger. Build a no-deal path using a documented plan, unaffected business units or similar independent firms. A useful peer faces similar demand, input costs and trends. A competitor that lost customers directly to the merged group may be affected by the deal and make an unreliable control. From the promised run rate to realized cash Some savings are already in baseline forecasts. A purchasing programme planned before the bid must not become a merger benefit after closing. Maintain a register of initiatives naming the action, cost base, start date, owner and any implementation outlay. Measure physical change and translate it to cash. Separate a full-year run rate from actual cash realized in the year. Then account for customers lost during integration, duplicated system costs, inventory investment, taxes and restrictions on timing. Use consistent prices or explicitly attribute favourable inflation instead of crediting management for it. What comparisons can and cannot establish A difference-in-differences comparison subtracts the change in a comparison business from the change in the merged business. When sizes differ, use comparable measures or suitable scaling. This method supports a causal interpretation only if the comparison would have tracked the merged business absent the deal and no different concurrent shock intervened. Deal selection complicates the exercise. Persistent problems may have led a company to be acquired just as its industry improved. Report the direction of potential bias and inspect trends before the transaction. A result near target profit can conceal costly risk taken to achieve it. title: Credit markets and rationing
detail: S02 · Lesson 1 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Study why a bank may refuse a higher rate. If safe borrowers leave or borrowers shift to risky projects, the lender’s expected return can fall. Selecting a customer pool A credit officer sees applications while entrepreneurs see their own projects. Imagine two business owners who both want €100. One expects a modest, almost certain sale. The other has a small chance of winning a large contract. Above a particular interest rate the first owner earns too little to apply. The second may still find the gamble attractive. This difference is present before the loan is signed. A bank that knows the population average but cannot identify each type must price the applicants who actually accept. Raising a quotation changes the population entering the contract. Historical defaults from last year’s customers may describe a different group. Why the return can bend down A limited-liability borrower keeps project proceeds above the promised repayment. Below it, the lender may take only what the business can deliver. This makes equity’s payoff steeper on the upside. A higher repayment can induce a funded borrower to switch to a more volatile project, even with a lower expected total payoff. The selection channel changes which people borrow. The incentive channel changes what an existing borrower does. Either can make a larger promise less valuable to the bank. When funds available at the bank’s best rate are below demand, some observationally similar applicants can go without credit despite offering to pay more. Finding evidence in a credit file To examine selection, compare applicants around rate changes, including people who refuse an offer. To examine incentives, observe project choices or risk-taking after disbursement. Both comparisons are vulnerable to a recession that simultaneously raises quoted rates and damages borrowers. Collateral or equity contributions can sometimes reveal commitment or affect incentives. Their usefulness depends on lenders being able to verify value and borrowers having wealth to pledge. A sound low-wealth applicant can be excluded by a collateral-heavy rule. Evaluate a posted rate Two quotations for equipment finance

title: Borrower and purpose
detail: S02 · Lesson 2 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Distinguish commercial, household and private-bank lending. A home mortgage, an inventory line and a securities-backed loan have different primary repayment sources. Identify the economic borrower The name signing the contract is the legal borrower. The business, person or property expected to supply repayment may be different. A holding company borrowing to buy a subsidiary relies on dividends or asset sales upstreamed from that subsidiary. A profitable subsidiary can still be unable to distribute cash when its own obligations are due. Draw the path from the external customer to the account that repays the lender. At each transfer ask who controls the money, which commitments come first, whether the currency changes and when it can legally move. A guarantee creates another potential claim with its own conditions. Match the instrument to the purchase Working capital buys stock or funds customer invoices. On completion of a cycle, collections can repay a revolving facility that becomes available for another draw. A productive machine typically releases its cost through years of operating cash. An instalment loan can spread repayment across those years. A mortgage on a home commonly depends on household income for scheduled payments. A private banking facility secured by traded assets can have a rapid margin call when asset prices fall. Similar collateral values across the two cases conceal different payment calendars and liquidation risks. Distinguish repayment from refinancing A bullet loan can appear affordable because the borrower pays only interest until a large terminal payment. Identify whether final proceeds come from a contracted sale, accumulated cash or a fresh lender. If a new financing market has to be open on one particular date, refinancing risk is material. A stated purpose can change after funds leave the bank. Draw conditions, supplier invoices and cash controls can provide evidence of how money is used. The value of each control depends on what it verifies and how early it alerts the lender to a change. Form the approval hypothesis One customer asks for a single bullet

title: The operating and cash cycles
detail: S02 · Lesson 3 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Trace purchase, stock, sale, collection and supplier payment. Seasonal working capital can support a revolver. Long-lived equipment usually needs a different maturity. Relate physical movement to financial statements Inventory days estimate how long goods sit before sale. Divide average inventory by cost of goods sold and multiply by the days in the period. Collection days use trade receivables and credit sales. Payment days ideally use trade payables and credit purchases. These denominators differ because invoices to customers include a selling margin. A report using closing balances from a holiday peak may systematically overstate typical days. Conversely, a quiet year-end can hide the peak funding requirement. Weekly or monthly averages, invoice aging and a purchasing calendar improve the interpretation. Two different clocks The operating cycle follows purchase, storage, sale and customer payment. The cash cycle begins when suppliers receive funds. Supplier credit shortens the interval during which the business needs its own or the bank’s money. A firm collecting customer deposits in advance can even have a negative cash cycle. A days calculation measures time. Turning it into euros requires the relevant daily flow. Use cost or purchases for stock and payables, and selling-price credit sales for receivables. Directly forecast cash by date when large deliveries, duties or advance payments make daily averages unrealistic. Seasonal and permanent needs A healthy seasonal revolver may build during the buying season and run down after collections. If it stays drawn after peak sales, examine whether stock is obsolete, customer payment is late or the business has grown permanently. Extending the line without understanding the change can fund hidden losses. A borrower may improve reported payment days by withholding overdue suppliers. This can ease short-term cash while threatening future deliveries. Ask whether terms were negotiated or simply breached and estimate how much funding would be needed if suppliers demanded prompt payment. Reconstruct the requirement Trading faster while needing more cash

title: Statements and cash available
detail: S02 · Lesson 4 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Reconcile reported earnings to cash after taxes, maintenance investment and changes in operating working capital. Document the definition of available cash in the case. Understand the bridge from earnings to cash A lender’s starting number determines the adjustments required. Starting from EBITDA avoids reversing interest and ordinary depreciation a second time. Starting from net income requires addressing tax, interest and noncash expenses already included in that number. Label the starting subtotal before touching the calculator. Earnings generated by an unpaid sale can increase profit immediately. If an invoice remains uncollected, the increase in operating receivables generally reduces cash relative to that profit. Conversely, an increase in trade payables may preserve cash during the period. Repaying overdue suppliers may produce the opposite effect later. Measure investment and recurring earnings A factory needs upkeep to produce future cash. Deduct maintenance capital expenditure even if management could briefly postpone it. Expansion investment may be discretionary or contractually unavoidable. Identify the case’s definition and timing before deciding how to treat it in a coverage analysis. A one-time cash grant, unpaid legal claim or profit on an asset sale changes the quality of the reported subtotal. Reconcile actual cash with a sustainable operating forecast. Identify which costs return next year. Sale proceeds themselves may be available for a one-off debt reduction even if recurring operating capacity is weak. Keep periods and claimholders aligned Cash flow available for debt service should be measured before the interest and principal in the denominator when both are treated as payment obligations. If interest has already reduced the cash numerator, adding the same interest again to the denominator understates capacity. Cash held in an entity restricted from transferring it may be unavailable to the particular borrower. Include only amounts available in the stated period and currency. A consolidated cash-flow statement can conceal restricted balances or financing provided by selling invoices with recourse. Build a reconcilable schedule A distributor’s forecast under scrutiny

title: Capacity and debt service
detail: S02 · Lesson 5 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Compare cash available for debt service with scheduled principal and interest. Test a difficult period because an acceptable annual average can conceal a missed instalment. Coverage and capacity are separate calculations Coverage describes a proposed payment schedule. Divide cash available by debt service over the same period. Capacity asks the reverse question, how much payment can cash support under a required coverage floor? Divide cash by the floor, then subtract payments already promised to other lenders. A coverage threshold such as 1.25 times belongs to the stated contract or credit policy. It is not a universal safe level. Volatile margins, customer concentration and bullet maturities can justify different sizing decisions for borrowers with the same current ratio. Turn a service limit into a loan amount A service limit is a payment, not a principal balance. For an amortizing fixed-rate loan, price the series of affordable payments. If each end-of-year payment is A, rate r and term n, the principal is A times [1 − (1 + r) to the power −n] divided by r. Check that the last payment clears the balance. A grace period that delays principal may increase early coverage yet leave a larger later burden. Evaluate peak service and terminal debt. A cash reserve can fund a temporary mismatch but does not produce recurring earnings. Specify whether its release is permitted under the lender’s terms. Test the dates before approving A six-month crop cycle can leave an exporter cash-poor at an interim coupon date even with excellent annual coverage. Use an opening balance and sequential cash roll-forward. Draw on a reserve only once and carry its remaining balance forward. A projected balance at a date before collection should exclude customer money that arrives afterwards. Stress the dates as well as the totals, for instance a late shipment or currency conversion, then examine whether a committed bridge or a revised repayment date is economically reasonable. Size a proposed facility A three-year amortizing offer

title: Default, exposure and severity
detail: S02 · Lesson 6 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Separate probability of default, exposure at default and loss given default. A borrower can draw an unused line or lose collateral value just when it becomes distressed. Loss probability and loss amount Default means failure under the definition used for this model, such as an unremedied missed payment. State the observation horizon, whether default is measured for the customer or facility, and the population being measured. A one-year probability cannot simply be substituted for a lifetime probability in a multi-year loan. Exposure at default represents what the lender is owed when the default happens. A credit card or revolver can be drawn further before failure. A conversion factor approximates the share of previously unused credit expected to become drawn. Repayments and contractual caps also affect exposure. Severity conditional on default Loss given default compares the economic shortfall with exposure once default has occurred. Include realistic proceeds, enforcement expenses and the time recoveries take. If collateral proceeds arrive two years after default, discounting can make the economic loss larger than a comparison of nominal principal and sale proceeds suggests. A guarantee can move part of recovery to a second obligor. The guarantee’s value depends on the joint event of borrower distress, guarantor capacity and legal enforceability. Adding both the full collateral value and a guarantee covering the same shortfall can overstate proceeds. Where the product formula comes from A performing loan contributes zero credit loss in this simple binary model. With probability p it defaults and loses some amount L. Average loss therefore equals p times the average loss conditional on default. EAD times LGD is a useful way to express that conditional loss when appropriately exposure-weighted or fixed. When exposure and severity move together within default scenarios, compute each scenario’s loss before averaging. Multiplying a simple average exposure by a simple average severity can conceal their dependence. Separate this expected loss from the tail loss that may determine available capital. Construct the loss estimate A revolver with delayed collections

title: Collateral, guarantees and priority
detail: S02 · Lesson 7 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Estimate realizable proceeds after costs and delay. Check collateral eligibility, seniority and concentration. A guarantee depends on the guarantor’s capacity when called. From an appraisal to distributable cash An appraisal answers a question about value at a particular date and under specified sale conditions. A lender’s recovery depends on a potentially different sale. Check asset ownership, an enforceable security interest, prior claims, insurance, currency and time needed to take control. An invoice face amount is just the opening input. Eligible receivables may exclude disputes, related parties, very late invoices and concentrations beyond contractual limits. A lender advances a fraction against eligible amounts to allow for collection risk and costs. That advance rate is a lending rule. Actual liquidation proceeds may fall above or below it. Work through priority one claim at a time Prepare a waterfall listing which claims receive available proceeds and what remains afterwards. Distinguish the proceeds of this specific asset from cash distributable across the wider borrower estate. Two secured creditors can have different ranks or share pro rata under the case terms. A guarantee introduces a separate potential payer. Understand limits, expiry, conditions to demand payment and the guarantor’s own financial resources when the borrower is distressed. A parent and its subsidiary may fail together. A guarantee on a shortfall cannot generate more than the remaining valid claim under the assumed terms. Time, currency and wrong-way risk Use one valuation date to compare near and distant recoveries. A sale worth €1m in two years buys less today than €1m now at a positive discount rate. Also model how a pledged asset correlates with the business. Shares in the borrower itself may collapse precisely when the lender needs to sell them. Valuation sensitivity informs monitoring design. Securities with frequent prices permit regular margin tests but may gap overnight. Special-purpose machinery can have a thin resale market. Liquidating it may depend on the very industry experiencing distress. Estimate an economic recovery A machine and a limited guarantee

title: Pricing the loan
detail: S02 · Lesson 8 · Lending and Credit Analysis
terms: Build a price from funding, operating costs, expected loss and a return for capital at risk. Distinguish a simple spread approximation from a full expected-value calculation. Build the lender’s economic account A lender parts with cash at origination, incurs funding and servicing expenses, and receives contractual or recovery cash later. Put all flows at the same date. A fee collected upfront reduces the amount actually funded. A fee payable only when the borrower survives belongs on the performing branch. Separate economic break-even from a target return. A lender charging for scarce equity capital may require proceeds above funding and expected operating cost. State whether a required capital return has already been incorporated in the hurdle to avoid adding it twice. Survival-weight the contractual payment For principal P, one-period default probability p, recovery R and promised rate r, expected receipts are (1 − p) × P × (1 + r) + p × R. Set this equal to the required terminal proceeds. This form assumes no interim payments and no interest in the default recovery beyond the specified R. For a multi-period amortizing loan, reduce outstanding principal after every payment and distinguish conditional default probability from survival to that date. Costs, late fees and recovery lags also have dates. Computing a single year’s spread only at origination need not price the full schedule. Decide which extra price is feasible A rate that clears the lender’s arithmetic hurdle may still make the borrower unable to pay, change the applicant pool or exceed what comparable facilities command. Apply a repayment-capacity test at the proposed contract rate and check that fees, maturity and collateral resemble the alternatives used as comparables. If the viable price range is empty, change structure or decline. Reducing exposure can lower risk concentration. Better reporting may reduce information costs. A guarantee can improve recovery but generally has its own costs and credit exposure. Quote from a common date An upfront fee changes the rate
